# Reconnection in 2D Inertial Magnetohydrodynamics

**Authors:** Lydia Boubendir Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 Email address: lydia.boubendir@princeton.edu , Peter Constantin Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 Email address: const@math.princeton.edu , Hezekiah Grayer II Address: Department of Mathematics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305 Email address: hezekiah@stanford.edu and Zhongtian Hu Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742 Email address: zh1077@umd.edu

## Abstract

We consider two-fluid equations of inertial magnetohydrodynamics in two spatial dimensions. These equations can be recast as the evolution of two active scalars, with fluid-like interaction kernels. The equations come in two flavors, left-handed and right-handed. They are conservative and have global unique solutions for both smooth initial data and for initial data in Yudovich class $L^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\cap L^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})$ . We prove that the inviscid limit holds in Yudovich class. We prove the persistence of $C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity of patch boundaries through merger events for the left-handed equations. We finally show numerical examples of magnetic reconnection, validating known rigorous results and uncovering new cases.

## 1. Introduction

Magnetic reconnection, a dynamical change of topology of the magnetic field lines, is a physical phenomenon of great importance to magnetohydrodynamics and plasma physics [3], [13]. The equations of ideal magnetohydrodynamics do not permit topology change in the absence of singularities. Magnetic resistivity can be responsible for a change of topology, but its time scale is in general too slow to explain the observed phenomena. A more rapid mechanism which does not require either singularities or resistivity was proposed in the physics literature [4], [6], [12]. The mechanism is due to inertia of electrons and it is described using fluid-like models with two fluids. The models are Hamiltonian, are derived from action principles and have been studied numerically, but not by rigorous mathematics, as far as we know, before the work [9]. That work was devoted to two-dimensional theory and proved regularity results and topological change due to merger of two active scalars.

The present paper is a continuation of [9]. We consider two-dimensional inertial magnetohydrodynamics where evolution of the electronic vorticity $\omega$ is coupled to the evolution of the magnetic canonical momentum $F$ . The system of equations is

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}F+\{\psi,F\}+\{\phi,\omega\}&=0,\\
\partial_{t}\omega+\{\psi,\omega\}+\{\phi,F\}&=0,\end{aligned}\right. $$

in ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ , where $\{f,g\}=\partial_{1}f\partial_{2}g-\partial_{2}f\partial_{1}g$ is the Poisson bracket. The electron fluid’s stream function $\psi$ is related to the vorticity by

$$ \Delta\psi=\omega, $$

and the magnetic potential $\phi$ is related to the magnetic canonical momentum by

$$ -\Delta\phi+\phi=\pm F. $$

The different $\pm$ cases are distinct, but are both conservative and derived from action principles. In [9] and in the present work, the $(+)$ case is called right-handed, and the $(-)$ case is called left-handed. Although only the right-handed system was considered in the physics literature [6], [12], both cases are mathematically interesting, yet quite different. Both systems can be re-written by a linear change of the dependent variables as evolution systems of two active scalars. Active scalars are real valued functions of space and time which evolve in time by pure transport, carried by incompressible velocities they instantaneously create. The velocities are computed from the scalars using time-independent, constant coefficient, and (in the present case) linear equations of state. The Yudovich class is the class of active scalars whereby (both) the scalars are bounded and integrable in space. Patches are particular cases, where the scalars are indicator functions of bounded domains in ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ . The Yudovich class is preserved in time, and weak solutions exist and are unique in it [9]. Each of the two flavors (right-handed and left-handed) has screened and unscreened versions. In the unscreened versions (3) is replaced by $-\Delta\phi=\pm F$ , i.e. the term $\phi$ is dropped. (That term physically corresponds to screening by an electronic skin depth).

The key feature of interest in the model (1) is the prediction of magnetic reconnection, i.e., topological change of the magnetic field $B=\nabla^{\perp}\phi$ , without resistivity. Until recently, this feature was only captured in numerical simulations [6]. In [9] the global well-posedness of (1) was obtained both in the Yudovich class and in the smooth category. Topological change was shown to occur in both the case of smooth solutions and patch solutions, and the results were for both the right-handed and left-handed systems.

In this paper we prove the convergence of solutions of vanishing resistivity to the solutions of the inertial MHD system (1). This is done by adapting the method of [8] to the case of two fluids. The result of [8] was for the two dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ , and extending it to the whole space presents certain challenges. One of the key elements of the result of [8] was the exponential integrability of the gradient of velocity. In Yudovich class the velocity is not Lipschitz-continuous, and the exponential integrability is a weaker surrogate for that. In the whole space, obviously there cannot be a global exponential integrability, and we have to localize the result. In addition, the decay of velocities is too slow for energy methods, and the velocities do not have self-contained equations like in the Euler and Navier-Stokes equations. We use methods form [10] to control decay at spatial infinity of the active scalars, in the resistive case, and overcome thus the technical obstructions to global Yudovich class zero resistivity limit. The proof is presented in Section 3.

The left-handed unscreened system consists of a pair of incompressible Euler equations which do not interact with each other. As it is known [5], [7], in the Euler equations vortex patch boundaries stay smooth through the evolution, if they start smooth. In Section 4 we show, for the left-handed screened system, that $C^{1,\alpha}$ - and $C^{2,\alpha}$ -regularity of patch boundaries persists globally, even through merger.

We conduct a numerical study of reconnection for patch solutions. In Section 5 we describe the algorithm, and in Section 6 we describe the results of the numerical simulations. These are as follows. For the left-handed screened equations, initialized by a disk and an ellipse, we show merger and then un-merger as the ellipse rotates through the disk, in complete analogy with the pure Eulerian dynamics of the unscreened equations. In the right-handed unscreened case, initialized by two patch disks with the same sign, we observe numerically translational merger. The patches travel along a common path and merge. When the right-handed unscreened equations are initialized by two patch disks of opposite signs, we observe orbiting patches deforming but not merging, indicating the possibility of (quasi) periodic solutions. We also show that the symmetry that was proved rigorously in [9] to lead to merger, does so numerically as well. Namely, we show that for right-handed unscreened and screened equations, initialized by four disks, with the same sign across the horizontal axis, and opposite sign across the vertical axis, there is merger across the horizontal axis.

## 2. The active scalar system

The sum and difference of the equations in the system (1) yield

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}(F+\omega)+\{\psi+\phi,F+\omega\}&=0,\\
\partial_{t}(F-\omega)+\{\psi-\phi,F-\omega\}&=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$

We define the scalars

$$ \sigma_{\pm}=F\pm\omega $$

and organize them into the vector

$$ \sigma=(\sigma_{+},\sigma_{-}). $$

The inertial MHD system (1) is thus equivalent to the transport equations

$$ \partial_{t}\sigma_{\pm}+\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)\cdot\nabla\sigma_{\pm}=0, $$

where in the right-handed system

$$ \mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)=\mathbb{U}(\omega)\pm\mathbb{B}(F), $$

and in the left-handed system

$$ \mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)=\mathbb{U}(\omega)\mp\mathbb{B}(F). $$

The operators are

$$ \mathbb{U}(\omega)=\nabla^{\perp}(\Delta^{-1})\,\omega, $$

and

$$ \mathbb{B}(F)=\nabla^{\perp}(1-\Delta)^{-1}F. $$

By construction, $\mathbb{U},\mathbb{B}$ and $\mathbb{V}_{\pm}$ have divergence free ranges. The operator $\mathbb{U}$ is the Biot–Savart law from the incompressible Euler equations, and the operator $\mathbb{B}$ is a screened version of $-\mathbb{U}$ .

## 3. The ideal inertial MHD limit

We first introduce the viscous version of (7):

$$ \partial_{t}\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu}+\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu}-\nu\Delta\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu}=0,\quad\nu>0. $$

This is the setting where the conductive fluid has momentum dissipation and ohmic dissipation of equal rate $\nu$ . The limit $\nu\to 0$ recovers ideal inertial MHD (1), or equivalently, (7). We show that any Yudovich solution of compact support to (7) may be recovered in this limit in a strong sense. We consider equal viscosities only for simplicity of exposition. The results hold for viscosities that vanish independently. We denote the space $\mathbb{Y}=L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and its product $\mathbb{Y}^{2}=\mathbb{Y}\times\mathbb{Y}$ .

We recall here information about the solutions.

#### Proposition 1.

We consider initial data $\tau=(\tau_{+},\tau_{-})\in\mathbb{Y}^{2}$ with compact support included in a ball of radius $L$ and we take an arbitrary time interval $[0,T]$ . We assume that

$$ \|\tau\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Omega_{\infty}. $$

The unique Yudovich solution of system (7) and the unique solution of (12) with the same initial data obey

$$ \|\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq V_{\infty} $$

where

$$ V_{\infty}=CL\Omega_{\infty} $$

with $C>0$ an absolute constant. We consider the ball

$$ B_{T}=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\left|\right.|x|\leq L\left(1+V_{\infty}\frac{T}{L}\right)\}. $$

Then, the support of the solution $\sigma(t)$ of (7) is included in $B_{T}$ . The solution of (12) with the same initial data obeys

$$ \|\sigma^{\nu}(t)\|_{L^{p}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus D_{T})}\leq C\|\tau\|_{L^{p}}e^{-\frac{LV_{\infty}}{\nu}} $$

for any $1\leq p\leq\infty$ and all $t\leq T$ , where

$$ D_{T}=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\left|\right.|x|\leq 9L\left(2+V_{\infty}\frac{T}{L}\right)\}. $$

We took $Re=\frac{V_{\infty}L}{\nu}\geq 1$ .

#### Proof.

The bound (14) follows from the Biot-Savart law and from the fact that $L^{p}$ norms of $\sigma^{\nu}$ are non-increasing in time. The proof of (17) follows the proof of Proposition 4 of [10]: the viscous solutions $\sigma^{\nu}$ obey bounds with exponential weights $e^{\frac{V_{\infty}}{\nu}\sqrt{1+|x|^{2}}}$ . The expanding domain is $\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\left|\right.|x|\leq 9L(1+Re^{-1}+V_{\infty}\frac{T}{L})\}\subset D_{T}$ . ∎

#### Theorem 1.

Let $\sigma=(\sigma_{+},\sigma_{-})$ be the unique Yudovich solution of system (7) with initial data $\tau=(\tau_{+},\tau_{-})\in\mathbb{Y}^{2}$ compactly supported in a ball of radius $L$ . Let $T>0$ be arbitrary and let $\sigma^{\nu}=(\sigma_{+}^{\nu},\sigma_{-}^{\nu})$ be the solution to system (12) with the initial data $\tau^{\nu}=(\tau_{+}^{\nu},\tau_{-}^{\nu})$ . Assume that the initial data belong to a ball in $\mathbb{Y}^{2}$ , and in particular,

$$ \|\tau\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Omega_{\infty},\|\tau^{\nu}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Omega_{\infty}. $$

Assume that $\tau$ is supported in the ball of radius $L$ and that (17) holds. For any $p\in[1,\infty)$ , if

$$ \lim_{\nu\to 0}\|\tau^{\nu}-\tau\|_{L^{p}}=0, $$

then

$$ \lim_{\nu\to 0}\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|\sigma^{\nu}_{\pm}-\sigma_{\pm}\|_{L^{p}}=0. $$

#### Remark 1.

In view of Proposition 1, the condition (17) is verified if the viscous initial data are compactly supported in a ball of radius $L$ .

The proof follows the pattern of the proof in [8], where the inviscid incompressible Euler limit was proved in the Yudovich class. Instead of scalar equations, we are now considering a system with two scalars. In addition, nontrivial adjustments need to be made because we are operating in the whole space, not on the torus. The velocity associated to a Yudovich $\sigma$ , even if the latter is compactly supported, typically decays only like $\frac{1}{r}$ , and thus fails to be in $L^{2}$ . Also, a key element of [8] was the global exponential integrability of gradients of velocity, which must be replaced here by local integrability. The strategy of proof is the same though. We prove a short time convergence on any time interval of order $c\Omega_{\infty}^{-1}$ if the initial data converge in $L^{2}$ and have the properties stemming from Proposition 1. We obtain the long time limit by taking many steps (of the order $T\Omega_{\infty}$ ). If we start from the same initial data, the inviscid solution will be compactly supported in $B_{T}$ and the viscous solution will obey (17) and in particular it will be exponentially small outside the fixed larger set $D=D_{T}$ , for all $t\leq T$ . We use these attributes of the solutions throughout the proof. We prove the result for the right-handed system. The proof for the left handed system is the same.

### 3.1. Proof for the right-handed system

In this section, we consider the right-handed system given by (7) and (8), together with the viscous version

$$ \begin{cases}(\partial_{t}+\mathbb{V}_{+}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla-\nu_{+}\Delta)\sigma_{+}^{\nu_{+}}=0,\\
(\partial_{t}+\mathbb{V}_{-}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla-\nu_{-}\Delta)\sigma_{-}^{\nu_{-}}=0.\end{cases} $$

Above, $\sigma^{\nu}=(\sigma^{\nu_{+}}_{+},\sigma^{\nu_{-}}_{-})$ for viscosities $\nu_{\pm}>0$ . The initial data is denoted $\tau^{\nu}=(\tau^{\nu_{+}}_{+},\tau^{\nu_{-}}_{-})$ . We prove

#### Proposition 2.

Let $\sigma,\sigma^{\nu}$ solve right-handed systems (7) and (22), respectively, with initial data $\tau,\tau^{\nu}\in\mathbb{Y}^{2}$ . Suppose that $\tau$ is compactly supported in the ball $B_{T}$ , assume both $\tau$ and $\tau^{\nu}$ obey (13) and that $\sigma^{\nu}$ obeys (17). Then if

$$ \lim_{\nu_{\pm}\to 0}\|\tau_{\pm}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\tau_{\pm}\|_{L^{2}}=0, $$

there exists a universal constant $C_{*}>0$ such that

$$ \lim_{\nu_{\pm}\to 0}\sup_{t\in[0,T_{*}]}\|\sigma^{\nu_{\pm}}_{\pm}-\sigma_{\pm}\|_{L^{2}}=0, $$

where $T_{*}=(C_{*}\Omega_{\infty})^{-1}$ .

Proposition 2 implies a more general version of Theorem 1 where $\nu$ is replaced by possibly distinct $\nu_{\pm}$ . To prove Proposition 2, we consider the transport of mollified initial data. We fix a scale $l>0$ and consider $\sigma_{l}=(\sigma_{+,l},\sigma_{-,l})$ which satisfies the system

$$ \begin{cases}(\partial_{t}+\mathbb{V}_{+}(\sigma)\cdot\nabla)\sigma_{+,l}=0,\\
(\partial_{t}+\mathbb{V}_{-}(\sigma)\cdot\nabla)\sigma_{-,l}=0,\end{cases} $$

equipped with initial data $\tau_{l}:=\varphi_{l}*\tau$ , where $\varphi_{l}$ is the standard mollifier at scale $l$ ; moreover, consider $\sigma_{l}^{\nu}=(\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}},\sigma_{-,l}^{\nu_{-}})$ which satisfies the system

$$ \begin{cases}(\partial_{t}+\mathbb{V}_{+}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla-\nu_{+}\Delta)\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}=0,\\
(\partial_{t}+\mathbb{V}_{-}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla-\nu_{-}\Delta)\sigma_{-,l}^{\nu_{-}}=0,\end{cases} $$

equipped with data $\tau_{l}^{\nu}:=\varphi_{l}*\tau^{\nu}$ . The transporting velocities are fixed; only the initial data have been mollified.

We decompose

$$ \|\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\sigma_{\pm}\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\sigma_{\pm,l}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\sigma_{\pm,l}-\sigma_{\pm}\|_{L^{2}}. $$

Because the transporting velocities are the same, the first and the third term above converge to $0$ as we send $l$ to zero, uniformly in $\nu_{\pm}$ . It remains to establish that

$$ \lim_{\nu_{\pm}\to 0}\sup_{t\in[0,T_{*}]}\|\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\sigma_{\pm,l}\|_{L^{2}}=0 $$

holds for a fixed $\ell$ . We note that the inviscid initial data are smooth and compactly supported and that the viscous solution obeys (17) (by the same proof). As a preliminary, we adapt two technical lemmas from [8]. The first one concerns the exponential integrability for the velocity:

#### Lemma 1.

Let $\sigma\in\mathbb{Y}^{2}$ with

$$ \|\sigma\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Omega_{\infty}. $$

Assume that there exists a compact $D\subset\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ such that

$$ \|\sigma\|_{L^{q}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus D)}\leq C\Omega_{\infty}|D|^{\frac{1}{q}} $$

holds for all $q\geq 1$ . Then, there exist absolute non-dimensional constants $\gamma>0$ and $C>0$ such that, for any measurable set $A$ we have

$$ \int_{A}\exp\left(\frac{\gamma|\nabla\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)(x)|}{\Omega_{\infty}}\right)dx\leq C(|A|+|D|). $$

#### Remark 2.

Note that the condition (26) is satisfied by solutions of the inviscid equations with $D=B_{T}$ and solutions of viscous equations with $D=D_{T}$ in view of (17).

#### Proof.

The proof follows from the observation that the condition (26) implies that $\|\sigma_{\pm}\|_{L^{p}}\leq C\Omega_{\infty}|D|^{\frac{1}{p}}$ holds for $p\geq 1$ . Then, expanding the exponential in power series and applying the Calderón–Zygmund $L^{p}$ bounds, and then choosing $\gamma$ small enough like in [8] concludes the proof. The zeroth order term introduces the dependence on $|A|$ . The first order term needs to be interpolated between the zeroth order and the second order, because the CZ estimate fails there, but this changes only the prefactor in the right hand side of (27). ∎

The second technical lemma is an adaptation of Lemma 2 in [8] for $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ .

#### Lemma 2.

Let $u(x,t)$ be divergence-free in ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ and assume that $\omega=\nabla^{\perp}\cdot u\in\mathbb{Y}$ obeys $\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\Omega_{\infty}$ and $\|\omega\|_{L^{2}}\leq\Omega_{2}$ . We also assume that there exists a set $D$ such that

$$ \|\omega\|_{L^{q}({\mathbb{R}}^{2}\setminus D)}\leq C\Omega_{\infty}|D|^{\frac{1}{q}} $$

holds for all $q\geq 1$ . Let a non-negative $\theta$ solve

$$ \partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta-\nu\Delta\theta\leq|\nabla u|\theta. $$

Then for $T(p)=\frac{\gamma(p-1)}{2p\Omega_{\infty}}$ and any $p>1$ , there exist constants $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ depending only on $\Omega_{\infty}$ , $\Omega_{2}$ and $|D|$ such that

$$ \|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq C_{1}\|\theta(0)\|_{L^{2p}}^{2p}+C_{2} $$

holds for $0\leq t\leq T(p)$ .

#### Proof.

We take a smooth, decreasing $p(t)\geq 1$ as in the proof of Lemma 2 in [8] and take the evolution of $\int\theta^{2p(t)}dx$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\int\theta^{2p(t)}dx \displaystyle=p^{\prime}(t)\int(\log\theta)\theta^{2p(t)}dx+p(t)\int\theta^{2p-1}\partial_{t}\theta\,dx \displaystyle\leq p^{\prime}(t)\int(\log\theta)\theta^{2p(t)}dx+p(t)\int\theta^{2p(t)}|\nabla u|\,dx. $$

Now we take a large constant $M$ and consider the set $A=\{x\mid|\nabla u|\geq M\}$ . We have that $|A|\leq\frac{\|\nabla u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{M^{2}}$ . On $A$ we use the inequality $ab\leq e^{a}+b\ln b$ with $a=\gamma\frac{|\nabla u(x)|}{\Omega_{\infty}}$ and $b=\frac{\Omega_{\infty}}{\gamma}\theta^{2p(t)}$ and Lemma 1. We obtain from (31) and (27)

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\int\theta^{2p(t)}dx\leq \displaystyle(p^{\prime}(t)+\frac{2\Omega_{\infty}}{\gamma}p(t)^{2})\int(\log\theta)\theta^{2p(t)}dx \displaystyle+\left[p(t)\left(M+C(|D|+C\frac{\Omega_{2}^{2}}{M^{2}})\right)+\frac{\Omega_{\infty}}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{\Omega_{\infty}}{\gamma}\right)\right]\int\theta^{2p(t)}\,dx. $$

We choose $p(t)$ to solve $p^{\prime}(t)+\frac{2\Omega_{\infty}}{\gamma}p(t)^{2}=0$ and conclude as in the proof of Lemma 2 of [8]. ∎

We apply this lemma to deduce an uniform in viscosity $H^{1}$ bound for the solutions of the transport of mollified initial data:

#### Lemma 3.

Let $l>0$ be fixed. There exists a universal constant $C_{*}>0$ and $C_{l}>0$ depending only on $l$ and $\|\tau\|_{L^{p}}$ , $p>2$ such that

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T_{*}]}(\|\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}\|_{H^{1}}+\|\sigma_{\pm,l}\|_{H^{1}})\leq C_{l}, $$

for $T_{*}=(C_{*}\Omega_{\infty})^{-1}$ .

#### Proof.

We show the proof of the bound for $\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}$ . Differentiating the first equation of (24), we have

$$ \partial_{t}\nabla\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}-\mathbb{V}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla(\nabla\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}})-\nu_{+}\Delta\nabla\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}=\nabla\mathbb{V}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}, $$

which implies

$$ (\partial_{t}-\mathbb{V}(\sigma^{\nu})\cdot\nabla-\nu_{+}\Delta)|\nabla\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}|\leq|\nabla\mathbb{V}(\sigma^{\nu})||\nabla\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}|. $$

Then using Lemma 2 with $\theta=|\nabla\sigma_{+,l}^{\nu_{+}}|$ and taking advantage of the fact that the initial data are bounded in $L^{p}$ with $p>2$ (paying in $\ell$ ) we conclude the proof. ∎

In order to prove (25), we note

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\sigma_{\pm,l}\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle=-\int\left(\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma^{\nu})-\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)\right)\cdot\nabla\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}(\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\sigma_{\pm,l})\,dx-\nu_{\pm}\|\nabla\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\nabla\sigma_{\pm,l}\|_{L^{2}}^{2} \displaystyle-\nu_{\pm}\int\nabla\sigma_{\pm,l}\cdot\nabla(\sigma_{\pm,l}^{\nu_{\pm}}-\sigma_{\pm,l})\,dx \displaystyle\leq C\Omega_{\infty}C_{l}\|\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma^{\nu})-\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T_{*};L^{2}(D))}+\nu_{\pm}C_{l}^{2}+C_{\ell}\|\tau\|_{\mathbb{Y}}^{2}e^{-\frac{LV_{\infty}}{\nu}}. $$

Indeed, the portion outside $D$ of the integral involving $\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma^{\nu})-\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)$ is bounded by an $L^{4}-L^{2}-L^{4}$ Hölder bound, using the boundedness of the velocities in $L^{4}$ , the bounds (33) and (17) with $p=4$ . We used Lemma 3 for the last term in the equality. In view of the differential inequality above, to establish the limit (25) and thus Proposition 2, it suffices to show that

$$ \lim_{\nu_{\pm}\to 0}\|\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma^{\nu})-\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T_{*};L^{2}(D))}=0. $$

In other words, it suffices to prove an analogue of Lemma 4 in [8] for $\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma)$ . We denote for simplicity of exposition the difference as $h=\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu}-\sigma_{\pm}$ and the semisum as $H=\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu}+\sigma_{\pm})$ . Let $\psi,\Psi$ and $\phi,\Phi$ satisfy

$$ \Delta\psi=h,\qquad\Delta\Psi=H,\qquad-\Delta\phi+\phi=h,\qquad-\Delta\Phi+\Phi=H. $$

In view of the definition of $\mathbb{V}_{\pm}$ , we rewrite it as

$$ \mathbb{V}_{\pm}(h)=\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{\perp}(\psi\pm\phi). $$

From (39), we see that (37) amounts to controlling $\|\nabla\psi\|_{L^{2}(D)}$ and $\|\nabla\phi\|_{L^{2}(D)}$ . We show how to control $\nabla\psi$ , the bound of $\nabla\phi$ is similar.

The equation for $h$ is

$$ \partial_{t}h+V\cdot\nabla h+v\cdot\nabla H=\nu\Delta h+\nu\Delta H $$

where $v=\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu}-\sigma_{\pm})=\mathbb{V}_{\pm}h$ and $V=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{V}_{\pm}(\sigma_{\pm}+\sigma_{\pm}^{\nu})=\mathbb{V}_{\pm}H$ . Consider a smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to 1 on a neighborhood of $D_{T}$ and compactly supported. More precisely, we consider $\chi_{R}:=\chi(\frac{|x|}{R})$ with $R$ sufficiently large and time independent, whose precise value will be made explicit below. For the ease of reading, we denote $\chi_{R}$ by $\chi$ .

We establish first some properties of $V,v,h$ and $H$ . For $h$ and $H$ , we have Yudovich bounds (time independent) and bounds which decay exponentially

$$ \|e^{|\cdot|\frac{V_{\infty}}{\nu}t}[|h(\cdot,t)|+|H(\cdot,t)|]\|_{L^{q}}\leq C_{q} $$

for all $1\leq q<\infty$ . Then with the above bounds, we show that

$$ |\psi(x,t)|+|\Psi(x,t)|\leq C\log R, $$

and

$$ |\nabla\psi(x,t)|+|\nabla\Psi(x,t)|\leq CR^{-1} $$

uniformly for $x\in\supp\chi$ . Indeed, to prove (42) it suffices to obtain the following estimate:

$$ \int\left|\log|x-y|\right||H(y,t)|dy\leq C\log R $$

for $|x|\leq R$ . For $|x-y|\leq 1$ we split $\log||x-y||\sqrt{|H(y)|}\sqrt{|H(y)|}$ and use $L^{2}-L^{2}$ to obtain $C\sqrt{\|H\|_{L^{\infty}}}$ from the first integral because $\log|z|$ is integrable on $|z|\leq 1$ , and $\sqrt{\|H\|_{L^{1}}}$ for the second integral. For the case $|x-y|\geq 1$ and $|y|\leq R$ , we use $L^{1}$ for $H$ and that $|\log|x-y||<\log R$ for $1<|x-y|\leq 2R$ . On the other hand for $|y|\geq R$ we use the fact that $|\log|y|H|$ is square integrable because of the rapid decay of $H$ .

To prove (43), it suffices to show that for $|x|\leq R$ ,

$$ \left|\int\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^{2}}H(y,t)dy\right|\leq CR^{-1}. $$

If $|x-y|>\frac{R}{2}$ , we bound $H$ by $L^{1}$ and the kernel by $CR^{-1}$ . If $|x-y|\leq\frac{R}{2}$ , we estimate the kernel in $L^{1}$ and use the exponential decay of $H$ .

We also need an estimate for $\Delta^{-1}\partial_{t}h$ . In conservative form we have

$$ \partial_{t}h={\mbox{div}\,}(-Vh-vH+\nu\nabla h+\nu\nabla H) $$

and use bounds on Riesz potentials,

$$ \|R\Lambda^{-1}(uH+Uh)\|_{L^{r}}\leq C\|uH+Uh\|_{L^{q}} $$

with $\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{2}$ with $q<2$ . We obtain that

$$ \|\partial_{t}\psi\|_{L^{r}}\leq K^{2}+\nu K $$

with $r>2$ and $K$ the Yudovich norm.

We take (40) and multiply by $-\chi\psi$ . After integrating by parts, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\int \displaystyle(\chi|\nabla\psi|^{2})dx=\int(\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla V\nabla\psi+Hv\cdot\nabla\psi)\chi dx \displaystyle+\int s(\nu)\cdot\nabla\chi dx-\nu\int(h+H)\Delta(\chi\psi)dx+\int\partial_{t}\psi\nabla\cdot(\psi\nabla\chi)dx $$

In the case of a single fluid $v\cdot\nabla\psi=0$ , but for two fluids the cancellation does not hold. Nevertheless, the term has a bounded multiplying factor $H$ . More care is required for the term with the vector $s(\nu)$

$$ s(\nu)=\psi(Hu-hU)-\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\psi|^{2}U+(V\cdot\nabla\psi)\nabla\psi. $$

The first piece is bounded in $L^{1}$ by $\log R$ times norms in $\|uH-Uh\|_{L^{1}}$ . For the second and third piece, we bound $|\nabla\psi|^{2}U$ in $L^{\infty}$ by $KR^{-2}$ after using (43), and bound $\nabla\chi$ in $L^{1}$ by $CR$ . Therefore

$$ \left|\int s(\nu)\cdot\nabla\chi dx\right|\leq K(1+\log R)R^{-1} $$

where $K$ depends on norms in $\mathbb{Y}$ of both $\sigma$ and $\sigma^{\nu}$ which are uniformly bounded and constant in time. The terms from the Laplacian when $\chi$ is not differentiated are $O(\nu)$ . Then,

$$ \int\partial_{t}\psi\nabla\cdot(\psi\nabla\chi)dx=\int\partial_{t}\psi\psi\Delta\chi\,dx+\int\partial_{t}\psi\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla\chi\,dx. $$

gives two terms. We use (42) and $\partial_{t}\psi$ in $L^{4}$ with (47) for the term $\partial_{t}\psi\psi\Delta\chi$ and have $\log R\|\Delta\chi\|_{L^{\frac{4}{3}}}=(\log R)R^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ . In the term $\partial_{t}\psi\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla\chi$ we use $L^{4}$ for $\nabla\chi$ and say $L^{3}$ for $\nabla\psi$ leaving $L^{\frac{12}{5}}$ for $\partial_{t}\psi$ . This term is thus bound by

$$ \left|\int\partial_{t}\psi\nabla\cdot(\psi\nabla\chi)dx\right|\leq K(1+\log R)R^{-\frac{1}{2}} $$

Now we estimate the term with $\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla V\nabla\psi$ . We split at height $M$ for the size of $|\nabla\psi|^{2}$ . We get a contribution of the form $KM^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ from the “bad” region:

$$ \int_{\{|\nabla\psi|^{2}\geq M\}}\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla V\nabla\psi\chi dx\leq KM^{-\frac{1}{2}} $$

This power comes from a priori bounds for $\nabla V\in L^{4}$ and for $\nabla\psi\in L^{4}$ . In the ”good” region we use the inequality

$$ ab\leq\epsilon e^{a}+\log{\epsilon^{-1}}b+b\log b $$

which follows from the familiar $ab\leq e^{a}+b\log b-b$ for nonnegative $a,b$ by considering whether $a\geq\log\epsilon^{-1}$ or not. If $a\leq\log\epsilon^{-1}$ then we obtain $ab\leq(\log\epsilon^{-1})b$ . If it is greater, we use the inequality $a^{\prime}b\leq e^{a^{\prime}}+b\log b$ for $a^{\prime}=a+\log\epsilon$ . We obtain an error $\epsilon K$ . Therefore

$$ \int_{\{|\nabla\psi|^{2}<M\}}\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla V\nabla\psi\chi dx\leq\epsilon K+\log\left(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}\right)\int\chi|\nabla\psi|^{2}dx $$

Overall, the right hand side of (48) is bounded by

$$ H_{\infty}\left[1+\log\left(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}\right)\right]\int\chi|\nabla\psi|^{2}dx+(\nu+y_{0})K_{0} $$

where we set

$$ (\nu+y_{0})K_{0}=\epsilon K+KM^{-\frac{1}{2}}+KR^{-\frac{1}{2}}\log R+K\nu. $$

with $y_{0}=\int\chi|\nabla\psi(0)|^{2}dx$ . This is obtained by taking independently and explicitly $\epsilon$ and $M^{-1}$ in terms of $\nu+y_{0}$ and $R$ in terms only of $\nu$ . (We could have done this for $M^{-1}$ and $\epsilon$ as well, but we need (and afford) them to be slightly larger.) We write

$$ y(t)=\int\chi|\nabla\psi|^{2}dx. $$

The diffential inequality is

$$ \frac{dy}{dt}\leq\left[H_{\infty}\left(1+\log\left(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}\right)\right)\right]y(t)+K_{0}(\nu+y_{0}) $$

Our integrating factor is $e^{-H_{\infty}(1+\log(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}))t}=e^{-H_{\infty}t}\left(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}\right)^{-tH_{\infty}}$ . We multiply by it and integrate

$$ \displaystyle y(t) \displaystyle\leq\left[y(0)+\frac{K_{0}(\nu+y_{0})}{H_{\infty}(1+\log(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}))}\right]e^{H_{\infty}t}\left(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}\right)^{tH_{\infty}} \displaystyle\leq(H_{\infty}+K_{0})H_{\infty}^{-1}(\nu+y_{0})e^{H_{\infty}t}\left(\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}\right)^{tH_{\infty}} $$

Now $\frac{M^{2}}{\epsilon}=K(\nu+y_{0})^{-A}$ with a fixed $A>0$ and for $AtH_{\infty}<1$ we have convergence to zero as $\nu+y_{0}\to 0$ .

We have shown the required convergence for $\nabla\psi$ in the inviscid limit, and a similar argument yields convergence for $\nabla\phi$ . In particular, (25) and thus Proposition 2 is proved. Theorem 1 follows via iteration, see [10].

## 4. Patch regularity for left-handed equations

In this section, we prove the propagation of regularity for the patch boundary in Hölder spaces. We show that the $C^{2,\alpha}$ boundary regularity can be preserved even when a $\sigma_{+}$ patch intersects transversally with a $\sigma_{-}$ patch.

### 4.1. Propagation of $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity

Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$ . We start with the propagation of $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity for patch solutions to the Left-handed, Screened (LS) model by following the approach à la [5]. We recall from [9] that the (LS) model can be equivalently formulated as

$$ \partial_{t}\sigma_{\pm}+v_{\pm}\cdot\nabla\sigma_{\pm}=0,\quad v_{\pm}=\pm\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\mp\mathbb{S}(F), $$

where $\mathbb{S}:=\nabla^{\perp}(\mathbb{I}-\Delta)^{-1}\Delta^{-1}$ , $F=\frac{\sigma_{+}+\sigma_{-}}{2}$ .

Following [5], we reformulate the patch problem as follows: let $\sigma_{\pm}=a_{\pm}\chi_{\Omega_{\pm}},$ where $\Omega_{\pm}$ are bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . We consider scalars $\varphi_{\pm}$ solving

$$ \begin{cases}\partial_{t}\varphi_{\pm}+v_{\pm}\cdot\nabla\varphi_{\pm}=0,\\
\varphi_{\pm}(x,0)=\varphi_{\pm,0}(x),\end{cases} $$

where $v_{\pm}$ can be explicitly written as:

$$ \displaystyle v_{\pm}(x) \displaystyle=\pm\frac{a_{\pm}}{2\pi}\int_{\Omega_{\pm}(t)}\nabla_{x}^{\perp}\log|x-y|dy \displaystyle\mp\left(\frac{a_{+}}{4\pi}\int_{\Omega_{+}(t)}\nabla^{\perp}_{x}G(|x-y|)dy+\frac{a_{-}}{4\pi}\int_{\Omega_{-}(t)}\nabla^{\perp}_{x}G(|x-y|)dy\right) \displaystyle=:\pm\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\mp\mathbb{S}(F) $$

where for $r>0$ , $G(r)=K_{0}(r)+\log r$ and $K_{0}$ is the modified Bessel function. Moreover, the patches $\Omega_{\pm}$ are given by

$$ \Omega_{\pm}(t)=\{\varphi_{\pm}(x,t)>0\}. $$

We assume that the initial domains $\Omega_{\pm,0}$ are defined as:

$$ \Omega_{\pm,0}=\{\varphi_{\pm,0}(x)>0\}, $$

where $\varphi_{\pm,0}\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and the following nondegeneracy condition holds:

$$ \inf_{x\in\partial\Omega_{\pm,0}}|\nabla\varphi_{\pm,0}(x)|\geq m>0. $$

We also introduce the following notations: since $\sigma_{\pm}$ is transported by incompressible flows $v_{\pm}$ , we set

$$ (L_{\pm})^{2}:=|\Omega_{\pm}(t)|=|\Omega_{\pm,0}|. $$

With the above notation, we record the following conserved quantities:

$$ \|\sigma_{\pm}\|_{L^{p}}=a_{\pm}(L_{\pm})^{\frac{2}{p}},\quad p\in[1,\infty]. $$

We also introduce the notations: given a function $f$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla f|_{\inf}:=\inf_{x\in\partial\Omega_{\pm}(t)}|\nabla f(x,t)|, \displaystyle|f|_{\alpha}:=\sup_{x\neq x^{\prime}}\frac{|f(x)-f(x^{\prime})|}{|x-x^{\prime}|^{\alpha}}. $$

We first show the following result concerning the propagation of the $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of $\varphi_{\pm}$ .

#### Theorem 2.

Suppose $a_{\pm}\neq 0$ , $\Omega_{\pm,0}$ , $\varphi_{\pm,0}\in C^{1,\alpha}$ , $\alpha\in(0,1)$ , such that (64) and (65) hold. There exists a constant $C>0$ depending only on initial data and $\alpha$ that the problem (61)–(64) has a unique solution $\varphi_{\pm}(x,t)\in C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ with the following bounds:

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}} \displaystyle\leq C\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}e^{Ct}, \displaystyle|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\alpha} \displaystyle\leq C(|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}t)e^{Ct+C_{0}e^{Ct}}, \displaystyle\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}} \displaystyle\leq\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}e^{e^{Ct}}, \displaystyle|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\inf} \displaystyle\geq|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\inf}e^{-e^{Ct}}, $$

for $t\geq 0$ , where $C_{0}$ is a dimensional constant.

The rest of this subsection is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 2. We arrange the proof into the following steps.

Step 1: Estimates for the singular part $\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})$ . Since the operator $\mathbb{U}$ coincides with the classical Biot-Savart operator for 2D incompressible Euler, we record the following results from [5] concerning Euler patches:

#### Proposition 3.

Let $\varphi_{\pm}$ be related to $\Omega_{\pm}$ as in (63) and (64). Then for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ , the following inequality holds:

$$ \|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\left(\frac{9}{2}+\frac{2}{\alpha}\right)|a_{\pm}|\left(1+\log\Delta^{\pm}_{\alpha}\right), $$

where

$$ \Delta_{\alpha}^{\pm}:=\frac{|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}|_{\alpha}L_{\pm}^{\alpha}}{|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}|_{\inf}}. $$

Moreover, we have the following result:

#### Proposition 4.

There exists a universal constant $C_{0}>0$ such that if $W_{\pm}\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathbb{R}^{2})$ is a divergence-free vector field tangential to $\partial\Omega_{\pm}$ , then

$$ |\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})W_{\pm}|_{\alpha}\leq C_{0}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\|_{L^{\infty}}|W_{\pm}|_{\alpha}. $$

Step 2: Estimates for the regular part $\mathbb{S}(F)$ . In this step, we first prove the following proposition concerning the regularity of $\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)$ :

#### Proposition 5.

Let $\sigma_{\pm}=a_{\pm}\chi_{\Omega_{\pm}}$ and $F=\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{+}+\sigma_{-})$ . The following bound holds:

$$ \|\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)\|_{H^{2}}\leq\|F\|_{L^{2}}. $$

In particular, the following bound also holds: for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \|\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)\|_{L^{\infty}}+|\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)|_{\alpha}\leq C_{\alpha}(|a_{+}|L_{+}+|a_{-}|L_{-}). $$

#### Proof.

To prove the proposition, it is more convenient to use the Fourier representation:

$$ \hat{\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)}(\xi)=\frac{\xi^{\perp}\xi}{|\xi|^{2}(1+|\xi|^{2})}\hat{F}(\xi). $$

Then by Plancherel’s identity and the above identity, we see that

$$ \|\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)\|_{H^{2}}^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(1+|\xi|^{2})^{2}\left|\frac{\xi^{\perp}\xi}{|\xi|^{2}(1+|\xi|^{2})}\hat{F}(\xi)\right|^{2}d\xi\leq\|F\|_{L^{2}}^{2}, $$

which proves (73). The estimate (74) follows from Sobolev embedding and (66). ∎

The following corollary then holds:

#### Corollary 1.

If $W\in(L^{\infty}\cap C^{\alpha})(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathbb{R}^{2})$ is an arbitrary divergence-free vector field, then

$$ |\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)W|_{\alpha}\leq C_{\alpha}(|a_{+}|L_{+}+|a_{-}|L_{-})(\|W\|_{L^{\infty}}+|W|_{\alpha}), $$

where $C_{\alpha}$ is defined in (74).

Step 3: Time-dependent estimate for $\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}$ . We prove the following result:

#### Proposition 6.

Let $T>0$ . Assume that $\varphi_{\pm}$ is a solution to (61) on time interval $[0,T)$ . Suppose that $\varphi_{\pm}\in C^{1,\alpha}$ and $|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}|_{\inf}>0$ for all $t\in[0,T)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\varphi_{\pm} \displaystyle(\cdot,t)|_{\alpha}\leq\left[|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}t\right] \displaystyle\times\exp\left(2\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)t+(C_{0}+1)\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}_{\pm}(\sigma_{\pm})(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right), $$

$$ \|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm,0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\exp\left(\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right), $$

$$ |\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\inf}\geq\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm,0}\|_{\inf}\exp\left(-\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right). $$

#### Proof.

From (61), we see that $W_{\pm}:=\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}$ satisfies

$$ \partial_{t}W_{\pm}+v_{\pm}\cdot\nabla W_{\pm}=\nabla v_{\pm}W_{\pm}. $$

Then estimates (77) and (78) follow on the Lagrangian paths of $v_{\pm}$ . We then focus on the proof of (76). By following an identical computation to that in [5], the following estimate holds:

$$ \displaystyle|W_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\alpha} \displaystyle\leq|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}\exp\left(\alpha\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right) \displaystyle+\int_{0}^{t}|\nabla v_{\pm}W_{\pm}|_{\alpha}\exp\left(\alpha\int_{s}^{t}\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s^{\prime})\|_{L^{\infty}}ds^{\prime}\right)ds. $$

Denoting $Q_{\pm}(s)=\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}$ and using estimates (72), (75), we further have

$$ \displaystyle|W_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\alpha} \displaystyle\leq|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}\exp\left(\alpha\int_{0}^{t}Q_{\pm}(s)ds\right) \displaystyle\quad+\int_{0}^{t}(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)+C_{0}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\|_{L^{\infty}})|W_{\pm}(\cdot,s)|_{\alpha}\exp\left(\alpha\int_{s}^{t}Q_{\pm}(s^{\prime})ds^{\prime}\right)ds \displaystyle\quad+\int_{0}^{t}(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)|W_{\pm}(\cdot,s)|_{L^{\infty}})\exp\left(\alpha\int_{s}^{t}Q_{\pm}(s^{\prime})ds^{\prime}\right)ds, $$

where $\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha):=C_{\alpha}(|a_{+}|L_{+}+|a_{-}|L_{-})$ .

Multiplying on both sides by $\exp\left(-\alpha\int_{0}^{t}Q_{\pm}(s)ds\right)$ and defining

$$ G_{\pm}(t):=|W_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\alpha}\exp\left(-\alpha\int_{0}^{t}Q_{\pm}(s)ds\right), $$

we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle G_{\pm}(t) \displaystyle\leq|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\int_{0}^{t}(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)+C_{0}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\|_{L^{\infty}})G_{\pm}(s)ds \displaystyle\quad+\int_{0}^{t}(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)|W_{\pm}(\cdot,s)|_{L^{\infty}})\exp\left(-\alpha\int_{0}^{s}Q_{\pm}(s^{\prime})ds^{\prime}\right)ds \displaystyle\leq|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\int_{0}^{t}(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)+C_{0}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\|_{L^{\infty}})G_{\pm}(s)ds \displaystyle\quad+\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)\|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\exp\left((1-\alpha)\int_{0}^{s}Q_{\pm}(s^{\prime})ds^{\prime}\right)ds, $$

where we used (77) in the last inequality above. Now applying Grönwall inequality, we arrive at

$$ \displaystyle G_{\pm}(t) \displaystyle\leq\left[|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)\|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\exp\left((1-\alpha)\int_{0}^{s}Q_{\pm}(s^{\prime})ds^{\prime}\right)ds\right] \displaystyle\quad\times\exp\left(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)t+C_{0}\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right), $$

Multiplying on both sides by $\exp\left(\alpha\int_{0}^{t}Q_{\pm}(s)ds\right)$ , we obtain the following estimate:

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\alpha}\leq \displaystyle\left[|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)\|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}\int_{0}^{t}\exp\left((1-\alpha)\int_{0}^{s}Q_{\pm}(s^{\prime})ds^{\prime}\right)ds\right] \displaystyle\quad\times\exp\left(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)t+C_{0}\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds+\alpha\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right). $$

Recall that $\nabla v_{\pm}=\pm\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\mp\nabla\mathbb{S}(F)$ and the bound (74), we have

$$ \|\nabla v_{\pm}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})\|_{L^{\infty}}+\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha). $$

Moreover, we have the bound

$$ \int_{0}^{t}\exp\left((1-\alpha)\int_{0}^{s}Q_{\pm}(s^{\prime})ds^{\prime}\right)ds\leq t\exp\left((1-\alpha)\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right). $$

Combining the above three estimates, we finally arrive at

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)|_{\alpha}\leq\left[|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)\|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}t\right] \displaystyle\quad\times\exp\left(\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)t+C_{0}\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right) \displaystyle\leq\left[|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\alpha}+\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)\|W_{\pm}(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{\infty}}t\right] \displaystyle\quad\times\exp\left(2\bar{C}(a_{\pm},L_{\pm},\alpha)t+(C_{0}+1)\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla\mathbb{U}(\sigma_{\pm})(\cdot,s)\|_{L^{\infty}}ds\right), $$

which yields (76). ∎

Using a Grönwall argument by invoking Proposition 6 and Proposition 3, Theorem 2 is proved.

### 4.2. Propagation of higher regularity

With the global-in-time propagation of $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity established in the previous subsection, we now concern ourselves with the propagation of higher regularity. For the sake of clarity, and without loss of generality we take $a_{\pm}=1$ .

To start with, we observe that Theorem 2 enables us to use the following Contour Dynamics Equation (see [9]): for all $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{+}(\alpha,t) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|\frac{\partial z_{+}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\tilde{G}(|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|)\frac{\partial z_{+}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\tilde{G}(|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|)\frac{\partial z_{-}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta, \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{-}(\alpha,t) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|\frac{\partial z_{-}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\tilde{G}(|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|)\frac{\partial z_{+}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\tilde{G}(|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|)\frac{\partial z_{-}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta, $$

equipped with initial parametrization $z_{\pm}(\alpha,0)=z_{\pm,0}(\alpha)$ , $\alpha\in[0,2\pi]$ . Here, the kernel $\tilde{G}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by

$$ \tilde{G}(r)=\log r+K_{0}(r)-(\log 2-\gamma_{e}), $$

where $K_{0}$ is the modified Bessel function and $\gamma_{e}$ is the Euler’s constant, enjoys the following properties: let $x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and denote $r=|x|$ .

- (1) (Far-field properties) $\tilde{G}\in C^{\infty}([1,\infty))$ . Moreover, the following estimates hold: for $r\geq 1$ , (83) $\displaystyle|\tilde{G}(r)|\leq C_{0}(1+\log r),$ $\displaystyle|\nabla_{x}^{j}\tilde{G}(r)|\leq\frac{C_{j}}{r^{j}},\quad j\in\mathbb{N},$ where $C_{0},C_{j}$ are universal constants.

- (2) (Near-field properties) For $r\in(0,1)$ , the following estimates hold: (84) $\displaystyle|\tilde{G}(r)|\leq C_{0}r^{2}(1+|\log r|),\quad|\nabla\tilde{G}(r)|\leq C_{1}r(1+|\log r|),$ $\displaystyle|\nabla^{2}\tilde{G}(r)|\leq C_{2}(1+|\log r|),\quad|\nabla^{3}\tilde{G}(r)|\leq C_{3}\frac{1}{r}.$ In particular, $\nabla\tilde{G}(r)$ is Log-Lipschitz.

The bounds (83) and (84) are known properties of the Bessel potential (see e.g. [1]). Finally, we introduce the arc-chord quantity

$$ |z|_{*}:=\inf_{\beta\neq\beta^{\prime}}\left|\frac{z(\beta)-z(\beta^{\prime})}{\beta-\beta^{\prime}}\right|. $$

We dedicate the rest of the section to proving the following main result:

#### Theorem 3.

Fix $\gamma\in(0,1)$ . Assume that $z_{\pm,0}\in C^{2,\gamma}(\mathbb{T})$ , $|z_{\pm,0}|_{*}\geq m>0$ , and $|z_{\pm,0}^{\prime}|\leq M<\infty$ . Then the system (81) admits a unique solution $z_{\pm}(\alpha,t)\in C^{2,\gamma}(\mathbb{T})$ for all $t\geq 0$ . In particular, for any $T>0$ , there exists $C(T)$ depending only on initial data, $T$ , $m$ , $M$ , and $\gamma$ that

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}(\|z_{\pm}(\cdot,t)\|_{C^{2,\gamma}(\mathbb{T})}+|z_{\pm}|_{*}^{-1}+|z_{\pm}^{\prime}|_{*})\leq C(T). $$

We start with showing the following bounds concerning a global arc-chord control and patch perimeter for $\sigma_{\pm}$ patches, which are consequences of the $C^{1,\alpha}$ theory. Such estimates are known for Euler patches, and we record them here for the sake of completeness.

#### Proposition 7.

For $\gamma\in(0,1)$ , let $\sigma_{\pm}=a_{\pm}\chi_{\Omega_{\pm}(t)}$ be the global $C^{1,\gamma}$ patch solution to the left-handed model (60). Let $\varphi_{\pm}\in C^{1,\gamma}$ be the patch-defining scalars corresponding to $\sigma_{\pm}$ satisfying (61). Define $\lambda_{\pm}(t):=|\partial\Omega_{\pm}(t)|$ to be the perimeter of the $\sigma_{\pm}$ patches. For any $T>0$ , there exists $C(T)>0$ depending only on initial data, $\gamma$ , and $T$ such that

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}\lambda_{\pm}(t)\leq C(T). $$

Moreover, let $z_{\pm}:[0,2\pi]\to\mathbb{R}^{2}$ be a $C^{1,\gamma}$ Lagrangian parametrization of the boundaries to the $\sigma_{\pm}$ patches. For any $T>0$ , there exists $C(T)>0$ depending only on initial data, $\gamma$ , and $T$ such that

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}|z_{\pm}|_{*}^{-1}\leq C(T). $$

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, we take $a_{\pm}=1$ . Fix $T>0$ . We start with proving (86). Since the scaling $\varphi_{\pm}\mapsto\mu_{\pm}\varphi_{\pm}$ , $\mu_{\pm}>0$ , holds the patch boundary invariant, we may choose $\mu_{\pm}>0$ appropriately such that the following gauge choice is valid: we select the initial parametrization $z_{\pm}:[0,2\pi]\to\mathbb{R}^{2}$ to be such that

$$ \partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta,0)=\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,0),0). $$

Note that this is indeed a valid regular parametrization since $|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,0)|_{\inf}>0$ . We claim that for any $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta,t)=\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t). $$

Indeed, on one hand, as $\partial_{t}z_{\pm}(\beta,t)=v_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t)$ , differentiating in $\beta$ we obtain

$$ \partial_{t}\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta,t)=\nabla v_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t)\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta,t). $$

On the other hand, from (61) we have

$$ (\partial_{t}+v_{\pm}\cdot\nabla)\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}=\nabla v_{\pm}\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}, $$

from which we obtain

$$ \partial_{t}\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t)=\nabla v_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t)\nabla^{\perp}\varphi_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t). $$

Then the claim follows from uniqueness for ODE. Hence,

$$ \lambda_{\pm}(t)=\int_{0}^{2\pi}|\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta,t)|d\beta\leq 2\pi\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}\|_{L^{\infty}}, $$

which concludes the proof of (86) after using (69), which implies that $\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|\nabla\varphi_{\pm}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}<C(T)$ for some $C(T)>0$ .

To show (87), we fix $\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in[0,2\pi]$ such that $\beta\neq\beta^{\prime}$ . We see that from $\partial_{t}z_{\pm}(\beta,t)=v_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t)$ there is:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2} \displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}|z_{\pm}(\beta,t)-z_{\pm}(\beta^{\prime},t)|^{2} \displaystyle=(z_{\pm}(\beta,t)-z_{\pm}(\beta^{\prime},t))\cdot(v_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta,t),t)-v_{\pm}(z_{\pm}(\beta^{\prime},t),t)) \displaystyle\geq-\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}|z_{\pm}(\beta,t)-z_{\pm}(\beta^{\prime},t)|^{2}. $$

From which we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}|z_{\pm}|_{*}^{2}\geq-\|\nabla v_{\pm}(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}|z_{\pm}|_{*}^{2}. $$

The above differential inequality plus (67) yields (87). ∎

For convenience, we introduce the following multilinear maps: given bounded vectors $a,b$ ,

$$ \mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z;a):=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\nabla^{i}\tilde{G}(|z-z_{\pm}(\beta)|)a_{i}\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta)d\beta, $$

$$ \mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z;a,b):=\int_{0}^{2\pi}(\nabla^{2}\tilde{G}(|z-z_{\pm}(\beta)|))^{ij}a_{i}b_{j}(\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta))d\beta, $$

We first show the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.

Assume that $z_{\pm}\in C^{1}(\mathbb{T})$ , $|z|_{*}>0$ , and $a,b$ are bounded vectors. Then both maps $z\mapsto\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z;a)$ and $z\mapsto\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z;a,b)$ are uniformly bounded and Log-Lipschitz. In particular, the following bounds hold: for any $z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , there exists some universal constant $C>0$ such that

$$ |\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z;a)|\leq C|a|\lambda_{\pm}(t), $$

and

$$ |\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z;a,b)|\leq C(\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}},|z_{\pm}|_{*})|a||b|, $$

Moreover, for $|z_{1}-z_{2}|<1$ ,

$$ |\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1};a)-\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z_{2};a)|\leq C\lambda_{\pm}(t)|a||z_{1}-z_{2}|\left(1+|\log|z_{1}-z_{2}||\right), $$

and

$$ |\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z_{1};a,b)-\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z_{2};a,b)|\leq C(\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}},|z_{\pm}|_{*})|a||b||z_{1}-z_{2}|\left(1+|\log|z_{1}-z_{2}||\right). $$

#### Proof.

We begin with estimates concerning $\mathcal{I}_{1}$ . The bound (92) follows from the fact that $\nabla\tilde{G}$ is a uniformly bounded kernel in view of (83) and (84). To show (94), we observe that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1};a)-\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z_{2};a) \displaystyle\quad=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left[\nabla\tilde{G}(|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|)-\nabla\tilde{G}(|z_{2}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|)\right]\cdot a\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta)d\beta. $$

Using (83), (84), and that $\nabla\tilde{G}(r)$ is Log-Lipschitz, we arrive at

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1};a)-\mathcal{I}_{1}^{\pm}(z_{2};a)|\leq C|a||z_{1}-z_{2}|(1+\left|\log|z_{1}-z_{2}|\right|)\lambda_{\pm}(t),\quad|z_{1}-z_{2}|<1. $$

This completes the proof of (94).

To prove (93), we define the set $E_{r}^{\pm}(z):=\{\beta\in[0,2\pi]\;|\;|z-z_{\pm}(\beta)|<r\}$ given $z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , $r>0$ . Then we decompose $\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}$ as follows:

$$ \mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z;a,b)=\left(\int_{E_{1}^{\pm}(z)}+\int_{\mathbb{T}\backslash E_{1}^{\pm}(z)}\right)(\nabla^{2}\tilde{G}(|z-z_{\pm}(\beta)|))^{ij}a_{i}b_{j}(\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta))d\beta=:I_{1}+I_{2}. $$

By (83), we note that $\nabla^{2}\tilde{G}(r)$ is uniformly bounded for $r\geq 1$ . Then it follows that

$$ |I_{2}|\leq C|a||b|\lambda_{\pm}(t). $$

To estimate $I_{1}$ , we observe from (84) that

$$ \displaystyle|I_{1}|\leq C\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}}|a||b|\int_{E_{1}^{\pm}(z)}\left(1+\log\frac{1}{|z-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}\right)d\beta. $$

To proceed, we claim the following bound for the set $E_{r}^{\pm}(z)$ : for any $z\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , $r>0$ ,

$$ |E_{r}^{\pm}(z)|\leq\min\left\{2\pi,\frac{4r}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}\right\}. $$

To show (96), we consider $E_{r}(z)\neq\emptyset$ . We choose $\beta_{0}\in E_{r}^{\pm}(z)$ . Then for any $\beta\in E_{r}^{\pm}(z)$ , we use the definition of $|z_{\pm}|_{*}$ to deduce that

$$ |z_{\pm}|_{*}|\beta-\beta_{0}|\leq|z_{\pm}(\beta)-z_{\pm}(\beta_{0})|\leq|z-z_{\pm}(\beta)|+|z-z_{\pm}(\beta_{0})|\leq 2r. $$

Hence, $E_{r}^{\pm}(z)\subset\{\beta\in\mathbb{T}\;|\;|\beta-\beta_{0}|\leq\frac{2r}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}\}$ and the claimed estimate (96) follows. With (96) and the identity

$$ \log\frac{1}{r}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\chi_{\{r<e^{-t}\}}dt,\quad r\in(0,1), $$

we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{E_{1}^{\pm}(z)}\log\frac{1}{|z-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta \displaystyle=\int_{E_{1}^{\pm}(z)}\int_{0}^{\infty}\chi_{E^{\pm}_{e^{-t}}(z)}dtd\beta\leq 2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\min\{2\pi,\frac{4e^{-t}}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}\}dt \displaystyle\leq C\left(1+\log\left(1+\frac{1}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}\right)\right). $$

Combining all estimates above, we conclude that

$$ |I_{1}|\leq C(\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}},|z_{\pm}|_{*})|a||b|. $$

This estimate together with that for $I_{2}$ yields the desired bound (93).

We finally prove (95). We fix $z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and let $\delta=|z_{1}-z_{2}|$ . Without loss of generality, we assume $\delta$ to be sufficiently small. Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z_{1};a,b)-\mathcal{I}_{2}^{\pm}(z_{2};a,b) \displaystyle=\left(\int_{E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})}+\int_{E_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1})\backslash E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})}+\int_{\mathbb{T}\backslash E_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\right) \displaystyle\left(\nabla^{2}\tilde{G}(|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|)-\nabla^{2}\tilde{G}(|z_{2}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|)\right)^{ij}a_{i}b_{j}\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle=:J_{1}+J_{2}+J_{3}. $$

To estimate $J_{1}$ , we note that for any $\beta\in E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})$ , we must also have $|z_{2}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|\leq 5\delta$ . Then invoking (84) we have

$$ \displaystyle|J_{1}| \displaystyle\leq C|a||b|\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}}\bigg(\int_{E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\left(1+\log\frac{1}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}\right)d\beta \displaystyle\quad+\int_{E_{5\delta}^{\pm}(z_{2})}\left(1+\log\frac{1}{|z_{2}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}\right)d\beta\bigg). $$

To estimate the first integral in the parenthesis above, we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})} \displaystyle\left(1+\log\frac{1}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}\right)d\beta \displaystyle\leq(1+\log\frac{1}{4\delta})|E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})|+\int_{E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\log\frac{4\delta}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta \displaystyle\leq C(|z_{\pm}|_{*})\delta\log\delta^{-1}+\int_{E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\log\frac{4\delta}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta, $$

where we used the bound (96) in the final inequality above. To estimate the integral in (98), a similar argument to (97) reveals the bound:

$$ \int_{E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\log\frac{4\delta}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta\leq C\frac{\delta}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}\left(1-\log\frac{\delta}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}\right). $$

Hence the above bound together with (98) yields:

$$ \int_{E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\left(1+\log\frac{1}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}\right)d\beta\leq C(|z_{\pm}|_{*})\delta(1+\log\delta^{-1}). $$

A similar argument also yields the following bound:

$$ \int_{E_{5\delta}^{\pm}(z_{2})}\log\frac{4\delta}{|z_{2}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta\leq C(|z_{\pm}|_{*})\delta(1+\log\delta^{-1}). $$

Summarizing the above bounds, we conclude that

$$ |J_{1}|\leq C(|z_{\pm}|_{*},\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}})|a||b|\delta(1+\log\delta^{-1}). $$

We then estimate $J_{3}$ . Given $z_{1},z_{2}$ fixed, we define $z(s):=z_{1}+s(z_{2}-z_{1})$ , $s\in[0,1]$ . Then we observe that for $\beta\in\mathbb{T}\backslash E_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1})$ ,

$$ |z(s)-z_{\pm}(\beta)|\geq\frac{1}{2},\quad s\in[0,1]. $$

Invoking the Mean Value Theorem and (83), we see that for any $\beta\in\mathbb{T}\backslash E_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1})$ , there exists $s(\beta)\in[0,1]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle|J_{3}| \displaystyle=\left|\int_{\mathbb{T}\backslash E_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\left[\nabla^{3}\tilde{G}(z(s(\beta))-z_{\pm}(\beta))\right]^{ijk}a_{i}b_{j}(z_{1}-z_{2})_{k}\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta)d\beta\right| \displaystyle\leq C|a||b|\int_{\mathbb{T}\backslash E_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1})}\frac{\delta}{|z(s(\beta))-z_{\pm}(\beta)|^{3}}|\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta)|d\beta \displaystyle\leq C|a||b|\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}}\delta. $$

Finally, to estimate $J_{2}$ , we observe that for any $\beta\in E_{1}^{\pm}(z_{1})\backslash E_{4\delta}^{\pm}(z_{1})$ , $|z(s)-z_{\pm}(\beta)|\geq\frac{3}{4}|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|$ . Hence by a similar argument to (100) using the Mean Value Theorem and (84), we have

$$ |J_{2}|\leq C|a||b|\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}}\delta\int_{4\delta<|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|\leq 1}\frac{1}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta. $$

We define $E_{j}=\{\beta\in\mathbb{T}\;|\;2^{j}4\delta<|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|\leq 2^{j+1}4\delta\}$ . Let $J$ be the smallest natural number such that $2^{J+1}4\delta\geq 1$ . Then clearly $J\sim\log\delta^{-1}$ . Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{4\delta<|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|\leq 1}\frac{1}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=0}^{J}\int_{E_{j}}\frac{1}{|z_{1}-z_{\pm}(\beta)|}d\beta \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=0}^{J}(2^{j}4\delta)^{-1}|E_{j}|\leq\sum_{j=0}^{J}(2^{j}4\delta)^{-1}\frac{16\cdot 2^{j+1}\delta}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}} \displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}\log\delta^{-1}, $$

where we used that $E_{j}\subset E_{2^{j+1}4\delta}(z_{1})$ and therefore $|E_{j}|\leq\frac{16\cdot 2^{j+1}\delta}{|z_{\pm}|_{*}}.$ Combining the above estimate with (101) we arrive at

$$ |J_{2}|\leq C(\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1}},|z_{\pm}|_{*})|a||b|\delta\log\delta^{-1}. $$

The desired estimate (95) then follows from (99), (102), and (100). ∎

With the technical preparations above, we complete the proof of Theorem 3. Recalling (81), we first write

$$ \partial_{t}z_{+}=\mathcal{F}_{1}+\mathcal{F}_{2}+\mathcal{F}_{3}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|\frac{\partial z_{+}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta, \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{2} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\tilde{G}(|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|)\frac{\partial z_{+}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta, \displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{3} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\tilde{G}(|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|)\frac{\partial z_{-}}{\partial\beta}(\beta)d\beta. $$

Fix $T>0$ . From the global in time propagation of $C^{1,\gamma}$ boundary regularity for any $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and Proposition 7, there exists $C(T)>0$ such that

$$ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}(\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1,\gamma}}+\lambda_{\pm}(t)+|z_{\pm}|_{*}^{-1})<C(T). $$

By [2, Proposition 4.7], we have the following bound:

$$ \|\mathcal{F}_{1}(\cdot,t)\|_{C^{2,\gamma}}\leq C(T)(1+\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{2,\gamma}}),\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

To estimate $\mathcal{F}_{2}$ , we observe that

$$ \partial_{\alpha}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{2}(\alpha)=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\left(\mathcal{I}_{1}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha);\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}(\alpha))+\mathcal{I}_{2}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha);\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha),\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha))\right). $$

Then applying (92) and (93), we have

$$ \|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{2}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C(T)\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{\pm}\|_{L^{\infty}}+C(T)\|z_{\pm}\|_{C^{1,\gamma}}^{2}\leq C(T)(1+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{\pm}\|_{L^{\infty}}). $$

Selecting $\alpha,\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathbb{T}$ such that $\alpha\neq\alpha^{\prime}$ , we further observe that

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\alpha}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{2}(\alpha) \displaystyle-\partial_{\alpha}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{2}(\alpha^{\prime})=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[\mathcal{I}_{1}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha);\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}(\alpha))-\mathcal{I}_{1}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime});\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}(\alpha))\right] \displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[\mathcal{I}_{1}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime});\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}(\alpha)-\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime}))\right] \displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[\mathcal{I}_{2}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha);\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha),\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha))-\mathcal{I}_{2}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime});\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha),\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha))\right] \displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[\mathcal{I}_{2}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime});\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha)-\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime}),\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha))\right] \displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[\mathcal{I}_{2}^{+}(z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime});\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime}),\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha)-\partial_{\alpha}z_{+}(\alpha^{\prime}))\right] \displaystyle=:\sum_{j=1}^{5}T_{j}. $$

Denote $\delta=|\alpha-\alpha^{\prime}|$ and assume without loss of generality that $\delta$ is sufficiently small. Using (104) together with (92) and (93) respectively,

$$ |T_{2}|+|T_{4}|+|T_{5}|\leq C(T)(\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{C^{\gamma}}\delta^{\gamma}+\|z_{+}\|_{C^{1,\gamma}}\delta^{\gamma})\leq C(T)(1+\|z_{+}\|_{C^{2,\gamma}})\delta^{\gamma}. $$

Invoking (94) and (95) respectively, we also have

$$ |T_{1}|+|T_{3}|\leq C(T)(\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{C^{\gamma}}+\|z_{+}\|_{C^{1,\gamma}}^{2})\delta\log\delta^{-1}\leq C(T)(1+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{\pm}\|_{C^{\gamma}})\delta^{\gamma}. $$

where the last inequality follows from choosing $\delta$ sufficiently small. Combining the above two estimates,

$$ \|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{2}\|_{C^{\gamma}}\leq C(T)(1+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{\pm}\|_{C^{\gamma}}). $$

A very similar argument also yields the following bound for $\mathcal{F}_{3}$ :

$$ \|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{3}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}\mathcal{F}_{3}\|_{C^{\gamma}}\leq C(T)(1+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{\pm}\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{\pm}\|_{C^{\gamma}}). $$

Using (105), (106), (107), and the equation for $z_{+}$ , we arrive at the following differential inequality:

$$ \frac{d}{dt}(\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{C^{\gamma}}+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{L^{\infty}})\leq C(T)(1+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{C^{\gamma}}+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{L^{\infty}}),\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

from which we obtain $\sup_{t\in[0,T]}(\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{C^{\gamma}}+\|\partial_{\alpha}^{2}z_{+}\|_{L^{\infty}})\leq C(T)$ . The same bound for $z_{-}$ is also obtained by a similar argument. This estimate together with (104) concludes the proof of Theorem 3.

## 5. The numerical algorithm

In this section, we validate numerically the theoretical finding of merger in the odd-even symmetry case, and explore potential mergers for other initial conditions. First, analytical representations are derived for four different initial conditions, as the basis for our numerical approximation. The approximation techniques we use are based on [11].

The initial boundaries of the vortex patches are closed curves in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , which we parameterize clockwise for $\alpha\in[0,2\pi]$ . We linearly interpolate the curves with $N$ nodes, which correspond to our discretization of the boundaries of our patches. The nodes are initially evenly distributed in $\alpha$ , and the contour is remeshed every $5$ time steps in order to maintain the uniform density of nodes (in $\alpha$ ). We then evolve the patches discretely using second-order finite differences to compute the differential contour element, second-order quadrature in $\alpha$ , and a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme for the time evolution.

In order to satisfy the CFL condition, we choose time-step:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta t=\frac{1}{N} $$

All numerical tests exhibit short-time convergence. We see no difference in behavior of patches evolved with $\Delta t=\frac{1}{N}$ and $\Delta t=\frac{1}{10N}$ . As in [11], we see that if there are too few nodes along the contour or if these nodes are spaced too far apart, the evolution of the discretized contour exhibits instability. After some time dependent on the initialization of the patches, the simulations become inaccurate as small scales form and the contour filaments. The numerical results we shall report are well before this time by an order of magnitude. In the results we report, the number of nodes is fixed to $N=512$ .

To visualize $F$ and $\phi$ , we solve an elliptic problem in the Eulerian frame. We mesh a relevant rectangular domain containing the contours throughout their time evolution and compute the values over time of $\sigma_{+},\sigma_{-}$ by evaluating for each time-step the scalar multiples by $a_{\pm}$ of indicator functions on the patches $\Omega_{+},\Omega_{-}$ in the interiors of $z_{+},z_{-}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\pm}=a_{\pm}\chi_{\Omega_{\pm}}(x) $$

$F$ is computed by taking the average of $\sigma_{+}$ and $\sigma_{-}$ .

For the right-handed unscreened system, we then compute $\phi=(-\Delta)^{-1}F$ using the fundamental solution of the Laplacian:

$$ \displaystyle\phi(x,t)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\log|x-y|F(y)\,dy $$

For the right-handed screened system, we compute $\phi=(I-\Delta)^{-1}F$ . Analytically we use the convolution of $F$ with the Bessel potential:

$$ \displaystyle\phi(x,t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}K_{0}(|x-y|)F(y,t)\,dy $$

where $K_{0}$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind of order zero. Similarly, for the left-handed screened system we compute $\phi=(\Delta-I)^{-1}F$ , introducing a minus sign to the above.

### 5.1. Translational merger

We start our numerical experimentation by looking at the right-handed, unscreened model in the case of the following initial conditions: set $\sigma_{+}(x,0)=\chi_{B}$ and $\sigma_{-}(x,0)=\chi_{\tilde{B}}$ , where $B$ is a disk centered at $(d/2+r,0)$ with radius $r$ . Here, $r,d>0$ . Also, $\tilde{B}$ is mirror image of $B$ across $x_{2}$ axis. Let $B$ , $\tilde{B}$ be parametrized by $z_{+},z_{-}$ , evolved according to the following right-handed unscreened contour dynamics:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{+} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}z_{-}(\beta)d\beta, \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{-} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}z_{+}(\beta)d\beta. $$

We use an explicit time-marching algorithm in order to advance the vortex patches every time-step. The contours of the vortex patches $z_{+},z_{-}$ are discretized into $N$ nodes. Let $z_{\pm,j}$ represent the $j$ -th node of each respective patch. We employ the trapezoidal rule to compute the integrals in (111), and second-order central finite differences to approximate the differential contour elements $\partial_{\beta}z_{\pm}(\beta)d\beta$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Delta z_{\pm,j}=\frac{z_{\pm,j+1}-z_{\pm,j-1}}{2} $$

We then sum the kernel interactions. See:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{+,i}\approx-\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum^{N}_{j=1}\log|z_{+,i}-z_{-,j}|\Delta z_{-,j} $$

Let this finite differences method be denoted $V(z_{+},z_{-})=(\partial_{t}z_{+},\partial_{t}z_{-})$ . To advance the position of the vortex patches in time, we utilize an explicit fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. For a given time step $\Delta t$ , the positions at the next time are updated as follows:

$$ \displaystyle(k_{1+},k_{1-}) \displaystyle=V\left(z_{+}^{(n)},z_{-}^{(n)}\right) \displaystyle(k_{2+},k_{2-}) \displaystyle=V\left(z^{(n)}_{+}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}k_{1+}\;,\;z^{(n)}_{-}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}k_{1-}\right) \displaystyle(k_{3+},k_{3-}) \displaystyle=V\left(z^{(n)}_{+}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}k_{2+}\;,\;z^{(n)}_{-}+\frac{\Delta t}{2}k_{2-}\right) \displaystyle(k_{4+},k_{4-}) \displaystyle=V\left(z^{(n)}_{+}+\Delta tk_{3+}\;,\;z^{(n)}_{-}+\Delta tk_{3-}\right) \displaystyle z_{\pm}^{(n+1)} \displaystyle=z^{(n)}_{\pm}+\frac{\Delta t}{6}(k_{1\pm}+2k_{2\pm}+2k_{3\pm}+k_{4\pm}) $$

As the vortex patches evolve, we remesh the contours $z_{+},z_{-}$ every $5$ time-steps using a periodic cubic spline interpolation in order to maintain even spacing between the $N$ nodes.

### 5.2. Antipodal disks

The antipodal disk scenario is evolved according to the right-handed unscreened system (111) where the contours $z_{\pm}$ bound patches of opposite sign. That is, we set $\sigma_{+}(x,0)=\chi_{B}$ and $\sigma_{-}(x,0)=-\chi_{\tilde{B}}$ , where $B$ is a disk centered at $(d/2+r,0)$ with radius $r$ . The contours $z_{+},z_{-}$ evolve according to the following system:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{+}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}z_{-}(\beta)d\beta, \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{-}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}z_{+}(\beta)d\beta. $$

The time integration, spatial discretization, and periodic remeshing protocols are identical to those described in Section 2.1.

### 5.3. Odd-even symmetry

In [9], a merger scenario is proved for the right-handed screened system with assumed odd-even symmetry. By odd-even symmetry, we mean the following symmetry:

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\pm}(t,-x_{1},x_{2})=-\sigma_{\pm}(t,x_{1},x_{2}),\quad\sigma_{+}(t,x_{1},x_{2})=\sigma_{-}(t,x_{1},-x_{2}). $$

The four patches we track are bounded by contours $z,-z,\bar{z},\tilde{z}$ where $\tilde{z}=(-z_{1},z_{2})$ and $\bar{z}=(z_{1},-z_{2})$ . The symmetry allows us to keep track of only one contour $z$ which is placed initially in the first quadrant, as the other three contours $-z,\bar{z},\tilde{z}$ follow by symmetry. We evolve $z$ according to the following equation:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}z \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left(\log|z(\alpha)-z(\beta)|+K_{0}(|z(\alpha)-z(\beta)|)\right)\partial_{\beta}z(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left(\log|z(\alpha)-\tilde{z}(\beta)|+K_{0}(|z(\alpha)-\tilde{z}(\beta)|)\right)\partial_{\beta}\tilde{z}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left(\log|z(\alpha)-\bar{z}(\beta)|-K_{0}(|z(\alpha)-\bar{z}(\beta)|)\right)\partial_{\beta}\bar{z}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left(\log|z(\alpha)+z(\beta)|-K_{0}(|z(\alpha)+z(\beta)|)\right)(-\partial_{\beta}z(\beta))d\beta $$

We also examine the right-handed unscreened system with the same odd-even symmetry. In the unscreened scenario, the contour $z$ is evolved according to the equation:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}z=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z(\alpha)-\bar{z}(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}\bar{z}(\beta)d\beta-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z(\alpha)+z(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}{z}(\beta)d\beta $$

Our algorithm computes the time marching of $z$ , which is then reflected across the $x-$ and $y-$ axes to visualize the positions of all four patches over time. The discretization and remeshing are identical to those described in Section 2.1.

In order to compute $F$ and $\phi$ in these scenarios, we see that the symmetry (116) implies that:

$$ \displaystyle F=\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{+}+\sigma_{-})=\frac{1}{2}(\chi_{\Omega_{z}}-\chi_{\Omega_{\tilde{z}}}+\chi_{\Omega_{\bar{z}}}-\chi_{\Omega_{-z}})(x) $$

Then, $\phi$ is computed numerically as described above.

### 5.4. Left-handed screened system.

In Constantin–Hu [9], merger is proven for the left-handed screened system modeled by the contour dynamics equation:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{+} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}z_{+}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\bar{G}(|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|)\partial_{\beta}z_{+}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\bar{G}(|z_{+}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|)\partial_{\beta}z_{-}(\beta)d\beta, \displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{-} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|\partial_{\beta}z_{-}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\bar{G}(|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{+}(\beta)|)\partial_{\beta}z_{+}(\beta)d\beta \displaystyle-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\bar{G}(|z_{-}(\alpha)-z_{-}(\beta)|)\partial_{\beta}z_{-}(\beta)d\beta, $$

where $\bar{G}(r)=-K_{0}(r)-\log r$ and $K_{0}$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind. The merger scenario is initiated by $\sigma_{-}$ a circular patch with intensity $1$ and $\sigma_{+}$ a Kirchoff’s ellipse with intensity 1. See [9]. Our algorithm is the same as previously described.

## 6. Numerical simulations

In our Figures, the leftmost plots show the positions of the contours $z_{+},z_{-}$ . ARTICLE

# The Risk-Priority View

Pietro Cibinel

Department of Philosophy, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, USA and Department of Philosophy, Princeton University, Princeton, USA Email: pcibinel@unc.edu

(Received 07 July 2025; revised 04 December 2025; accepted 03 January 2026)

Abstract This paper develops and defends a non-utilitarian interpretation of John Harsanyi’s social aggregation theorem and sum of vNM utilities approach. On this interpretation, vNM utilities transform an independently available cardinal measure of fully comparable individual well-being. The resulting proposal for ranking well-being distributions – the Risk-Priority View – is not welfare-anonymous and can favour a smaller increase in wellbeing for one individual rather than a larger increase in well-being for another, equally well-off individual. I argue here that such counterintuitive implications can be defended, and that impartiality can still be secured through the imposition of an alternative, interprofile anonymity axiom.

Keywords: Harsanyi’s social aggregation theorem; Sen–Weymark critique; vNM utility; well-being; distributive ethics

1. Introduction How should we evaluate distributions of well-being across people? The simplest approach is Utilitarianism: the value of a distribution is given by summing each person’s well-being. Another common approach is the Priority View, or Prioritarianism: the value of a distribution is given by first transforming each person’s well-being in a certain way, and then summing such transformed wellbeing levels. The prioritarian transformation is the same for all individuals, and ends up giving more weight to worse-off people (Parfit 2002; Adler 2011). A central argument for Utilitarianism is given by John Harsanyi’s interpretation of his social aggregation theorem (1955, 1977, 1982). Harsanyi shows that if individual and social preferences in conditions of risk satisfy the axioms of expected utility theory, and if social preference defers to individual preferences when the latter all agree, then there exist von Neumann–Morgenstern (vNM) expected utility representations V; V1; . . . ; Vn for society and individual preferences respectively, such that

(following Broome’s 2015 statement). Lotteries and hence degenerate lotteries – i.e. outcomes – are ranked according to a sum of vNM utilities. Harsanyi went on to interpret the individual vNM utility representations in this formula as cardinal measures of individual well-being. He therefore took his theorem to support Utilitarianism: if outcomes are ranked by a sum of individual vNM utilities, and the latter are cardinal measures of well-being, then outcomes are ranked by summing individual well-being. However, Harsanyi’s interpretation of his social aggregation theorem is contentious. According to what has come to be known as the Sen–Weymark critique (Sen 1976, 1977; Weymark 1991; Roemer 1996), the cardinal structure that individual well-being has (or may have) is to be sharply distinguished conceptually from the quantity that the vNM representation theorem identifies, i.e. which individuals that satisfy the vNM axioms maximize in expectation (von Neumann Morgenstern 1944; see Fishburn 1989). Absent an argument for why the two should be identified, Harsanyi’s aggregation theorem fails to support Utilitarianism. There are different ways one can react to the Sen–Weymark critique. One option is to claim that well-being has no cardinal structure independently of vNM utility; hence there is only really one quantity, vNM utility, and it provides a precisification of what we might mean by “quantities of well-being” and “utilitarianism”.1 Another option is to insist that well-being does have cardinal structure independently of vNM utility, and reject the sum of vNM utility approach (more on this below).2

This paper explores a different route. Suppose we assume that well-being has cardinal structure independently of vNM utility and is comparable across individuals, and that individuals’ preferences can display differing degrees of risk-aversion in wellbeing, as encoded by their vNM utility.3 We can then ask two sets of questions. First, what position do we land on, with respect to the question of how well-being itself (as opposed to income or resources) should be distributed? That is, how should we then interpret the sum of vNM utilities vis-à-vis the project of ranking well-being distributions? Second, could we still defensibly maintain that social value is given by a sum of vNM utilities? Can the resulting position be morally justified? The large literature surrounding Harsanyi’s aggregation theorem seems to lack a sustained philosophical investigation of these questions, especially with regard to the latter set.4

I will treat the Sen–Weymark critique as a point of departure to investigate whether a non-utilitarian philosophical defence of the sum of vNM utility approach can be given on the assumption that well-being is cardinally measurable and comparable independently of vNM utility. I develop and defend an alternative interpretation of the philosophical significance of Harsanyi’s social aggregation theorem. Like Prioritarianism, the ranking of well-being distributions that I claim is supported by Harsanyi’s social aggregation theorem evaluates each distribution of well-being in terms of a sum of transformed well-being levels. Unlike Prioritarianism, it does not perform the same transformation for all individuals, for the simple reason that people’s preferences under risk with respect to well-being may differ: what transformation is performed on an individual’s well-being level depends on that individual’s attitude to risks involving well-being. We can call this a

Risk-Prioritarian interpretation of the sum of vNM utilities. Social value is a sum of transformed well-being levels such that each individual’s transformation function is determined by their risk attitude in well-being, with risk attitudes in well-being allowed to vary across individuals.

Is this reinterpretation of the sum of vNM utility approach philosophically viable? An obvious difficulty is that when people’s risk attitudes for well-being differ, as they can be expected to, the Risk-Prioritarian interpretation entails that individuals should receive differential treatment in well-being (see Blackorby et al. 1980: 30; Cibinel 2025b). This contravenes deeply held intuitions. It is standardly believed that

(OUTCOME ANONYMITY) if the well-being distributions of two outcomes x and y only differ in who gets which well-being level, x and y are equally good (see e.g. Adler 2019: 97),

and, even more strongly, that

(SUPPES–SEN PRINCIPLE) if the well-being distributions of two outcomes x and y only differ in who gets which well-being level, and we improve the well-being of some individuals in x to get x, then x is better than y (adapting Suppes 1966; Sen 2017: 211).

To think otherwise, it is typically said, amounts to being objectionably partial: to prioritize the interest of some individuals just because of their identity. Utilitarianism, Prioritarianism and all the other main rankings of well-being distributions satisfy these principles. I will argue, however, that the Risk-Prioritarian rejection of Outcome Anonymity and the Suppes–Sen Principle can be defended. The Risk-Priority View denies these principles not because it thinks some individuals’ well-being matters more simpliciter, but rather because it thinks their well-being matters more in some specific cases, and the well-being of other individuals matters more in other cases. It is a differential treatment that is compatible with, and indeed secures, impartiality.5
