Here is how the paper will be structured. In section 2, I develop the Risk- Prioritarian interpretation in full detail. In section 3, I discuss the issue of vNM utility comparisons in light of the Risk-Prioritarian interpretation. In section 4, I proceed to develop two interrelated philosophical defences of the Risk-Prioritarian rejection of Outcome Anonymity and the Suppes–Sen Principle. Section 5 concludes the paper, and is followed by a formal Appendix. Before I proceed, a note on the scope of this paper. My aim is to argue that the Risk-Prioritarian interpretation of the sum of vNM utility approach is philosophically tenable, in the sense that its counterintuitive ranking of wellbeing distributions can be defended. To my knowledge, no other work in the literature argues for the plausibility of the sum of vNM utility approach in the face of an explicit assumption of cardinal well-being measurability and comparability independent of vNM utility itself, with vNM utility obtained from heterogeneous individual preferences over well-being lotteries. This is the distinctive contribution of the paper. I do not attempt to defend the sum of vNM utility approach in general as against a range of objections stemming from alternative approaches one might take in social ethics, and in response to Harsanyi’s aggregation theorem. A few such approaches, however, deserve mention. Ex post versions of prioritarianism as well as non-separable egalitarianism reject the application of Pareto principles ex ante, because of the resulting insensitivity to the distribution of well-being ex post (see Adler 2011: Ch. 7; 2025: 241; Voorhoeve and Fleurbaey 2013; Adler and Holtug 2019). Ex ante versions of prioritarianism and non-separable egalitarianism, by contrast, reject the application of expected utility theory (indeed, of weaker dominance principles) at the level of social preference; relevant here is Diamond’s (1967) early critique of Harsanyi, showing that the sum of vNM utility approach cannot accommodate a kind of “fairness” in the distribution of probabilities of wellbeing improvements and losses (see Epstein and Segal 1992; McCarthy 2006; for applied comparisons between the ex ante and ex post prioritarian approaches see Adler et al. 2021 and Ferranna et al. 2023). A sum of vNM utility proponent certainly needs to reckon with such alternatives, but they can do so independently of how vNM utility is understood: whether as a cardinal measure of well-being, as per the utilitarian interpretation, or as a transformation on well-being, as per the Risk- Prioritarian interpretation. This brief tour of alternatives should, however, underscore how different Risk-Prioritarianism is from traditional strands of prioritarian thought.

We then consider the set of probability functions on the set of outcomes, and interpret such functions as the policies or “lotteries” with possibly uncertain outcomes that we want to evaluate socially.7 We can now treat any outcome x as equivalent to the “degenerate” probability function that assigns probability 1 to x and 0 to all other outcomes. Each lottery a gives to each individual i a prospect ai: a probability function over well-being levels. We are interested in individuals’ preferences over prospects. We assume that they are orderings – that is, complete and transitive relations. Moreover, we assume that when restricted to degenerate prospects, these orderings match (the ordering of) well-being levels: a degenerate prospect is preferred to another just in case it results in greater well-being. We will be asking whether our evaluations of policies should change upon variations in people’s preferences over prospects – that is, changes in their risk attitudes in well-being. To address this, we need to consider different configurations of possible preferences over prospects that individuals might have. We will think of these as lists, with n entries, of orderings of prospects, and call them risk profiles, or simply profiles. The set of all risk profiles of interest will be denoted by R. Impartial Risk-Prioritarianism is characterized via the introduction of a second, new axiom, which I will call Interprofile Anonymity. I will first illustrate how the axiom works with an example. Suppose that there are three individuals, Cam, Dale, and Elise. We consider two risk profiles, R and R0. Under R, Cam is risk-averse, Dale risk-seeking and Elise risk-neutral. Under R0, Cam and Dale swap risk attitudes: Cam is risk-seeking (to the same degree that Dale is in R), Dale is risk-averse (to the same degree that Cam is in R), and Elise is again risk-neutral. Consider now four lotteries a; b; c; d with sure outcomes, where w > w > w are numbers representing quantities of well-being (Figure 1). Notice that Elise is unaffected in a comparison between the four lotteries; so, we can forget about the last column in the table. Suppose c is socially better than a under R. This means that the gain of giving w to risk-seeking Dale more than makes up for the loss of giving w to risk-averse Cam under R. R0 differs only in that we swap Cam and Dale’s risk attitudes. 3. Scaling of vNM Functions The crucial question now to be considered is how exactly vNM utility functions should be scaled in the framework of section 2. This question arises for all proponents of the view that social value is given by a sum of vNM utilities. But it means something different on a Risk-Prioritarian interpretation of such a sum than it does on a utilitarian interpretation. On a utilitarian interpretation of Harsanyi’s aggregation theorem, scaling vNM utility functions amounts to deciding how to make comparisons of well-being improvements and losses for different people (see Adler 2019: 55–64; Fleurbaey and Zuber 2021). On the Risk-Prioritarian interpretation, scaling vNM utility functions amounts to deciding how to make comparisons of the moral significance of well-being improvements and losses for people with different risk attitudes in well-being.15

What the Risk-Prioritarian interpretation of Harsanyi’s aggregation theorem developed in section 2 gives us is thus a class of theories, which differ from one another in the way they make interpersonal comparisons of vNM utility for people with different risk attitudes in well-being. There is an analogy here with Prioritarianism. The Priority View is also a class of theories, with each member of this class differing from the others in the degree to which it prioritizes worse-off individuals. Some prioritarian theories implausibly give too much – or too little – weight to the worse off. While the class of Prioritarian rankings can be characterized axiomatically (Adler 2022: 63), particular normative judgements have to guide prioritarians in making their choice of which version of their theory to accept.

15Of course, utilitarians see no difference between quantities of well-being and how much these quantities count (Broome 1991). But non-utilitarians disagree: according to a prioritarian, for example, an equal improvement in well-being matters more, morally, the worse off an individual is (Parfit 2002; Adler 2011). Greaves (2015: 587) calls “modern utilitarianism” the view that vNM utility equals (what I have been calling) moral significance. On this taxonomy, both Harsanyi’s Utilitarianism and the Risk-Priority View count as versions of “modern utilitarianism”. It seems to me that most modern utilitarians in this sense are either squarely followers of Harsanyi, or at any rate fail to take seriously the idea that there could be quantities of well-being independently of vNM utility (see Greaves 2017). A case that I find hard to categorize is Hammond (1996). His theory sums individual vNM utilities, where these are derived from ethical choices that bear upon each individual singly; unlike Harsanyi, he explains that these quantities are not what classical utilitarians have in mind, and rather have “purely ethical significance” (94). He nonetheless calls each individual’s vNM utility so understood their “welfare” (94). I am unsure how many “modern utilitarians” would side with the Risk-Priority View if they became convinced of its assumption that we can make sense of quantities of well-being independently of vNM utility, and how many would instead cling to the truly utilitarian aspect of their position and side with Utilitarianism. As I hope to clarify with this paper, the two alternatives have very different motivations.

An intuitive case for this scaling can be made along the following lines. There are different ways to pursue one’s good (well-being) under risk: risk-averse individuals focus on avoiding worse case scenarios; risk-seeking individuals focus on pursuing better case scenarios. For this reason, it is somewhat worse if risk-averse people end up very poorly off, compared to risk-seeking ones. And it is to some extent better if risk-seeking people end up very well off, compared to risk-averse ones. Crucially, it is not worse for the individuals in question: on the Risk-Prioritarian (unlike on the utilitarian) interpretation of vNM utility, cardinally measurable and comparable well-being levels are what people’s vNM utility functions take as arguments. Rather, the claim is that these outcomes are worse or better from a moral or social point of view (compare Nebel 2022: 39). Thus, for instance, going from wL to wL  Δ is exactly as bad for a risk-averse individual as it is for a risk-seeking individual, by design of our section 2 setup. 4. The Risk-Priority Ethos While Interprofile Anonymity sweetens the pill of Risk-Prioritarian violations of Outcome Anonymity and the Suppes–Sen Principle, the task remains of providing a philosophically compelling story for why people’s well-being should be weighed differently, according to their risk attitude, even in risk-free cases. Fundamentally, what motivates taking account of risk attitudes when there is no risk involved? Ostensibly, Strong Pareto only recommends giving weight to risk attitudes in risky contexts. The counterintuitive Risk-Prioritarian violations of Outcome Anonymity and the Suppes–Sen Principle, by contrast, result from giving weight to risk attitudes in risk-free contexts. What philosophical move could possibly get us from the former stance to the latter? This section pursues two interrelated answers, concerning justifiability to each person and individual responsibility, respectively. To keep things simple, I will focus on violations of Outcome Anonymity; my remarks generalize to violations of the Suppes–Sen Principle. The strategy is this: I will introduce cases that proponents of Strong Pareto should already recognize as supporting some form of differential weighting of well-being, and describe how these verdicts are typically motivated. I will then show that such standard justifications of these verdicts should be developed and built upon in ways that lead to more radical violations of Outcome Anonymity, involving risk-free contexts. It might be suggested that we need to know what would have happened had she chosen otherwise: if, had she chosen in the same way as Bruno, she would have ended up safe at well-being level wL, then she is responsible for her actual bad condition; but if, had she chosen in that way, she would still have ended up at well-being level wL  Δ, then she is not responsible for her actual bad condition. But, first, there may be no fact of the matter as to what would have happened had Alda chosen otherwise (see Hare 2011, 2015). And, second, answering this question does not seem normatively relevant after all. Suppose the 50% background chance that Alda and Bruno end up at well-being level wL  Δ in Background Risk is due to the presence of an incoming storm, which carries the threat of being hit by lightning.

Each of them can stay at home: lightning will hit their house with 50% probability, but there is nowhere more protected where they can go. If their house remains intact, they will be safe but bored, at well-being level wL. Alternatively, they can go out surfing. If all goes well, they enjoy themselves, at well-being level wG  Δ; however, going surfing increases the chance of being hit by lightning to 75%. Alda goes surfing and gets hit by lighning. Suppose that Bruno, who stays home, is also hit by lightning. If we only have the resources to provide first-aid care to one of them, who should we help? I think the answer is that Bruno should be prioritized. And this is so even if we learn ex post that, had Alda remained at home, she would have been hit by lightning anyway. What matters to assessing Alda’s situation, it seems to me, is that she chose to run more risk than Bruno did.25

The discussion does show, nonetheless, that the sense in which Alda is responsible for her bad condition in Background Risk is rather sui generis, and quite distinct from the more familiar notion of moral responsibility employed in attributions of praise and blame. Alda’s odds were not ideal to start with, since she faced a 50% background risk that she could not get rid of. And it’s not as if she wanted risk for its own sake: had she had the option of securing well-being level wG  Δ with certainty – going surfing with a clear sky – she would have chosen that. Taking a gamble means that we are acting in sub-optimal circumstances, which must be taken into account when evaluating responsibility for risks incurred. This points to the suggestion that we interpret Alda’s responsibility for her bad condition comparatively, to mean that she should receive less priority, in this case, than people in similar circumstances who took fewer risks, and that the reason for this is precisely that she chose to be more risk-seeking than those other people. That choice was hers, and in this sense she is responsible for it. But this does not mean that, if we can help her at no cost to others, we have no reason to do so (cf. Lippert-Rasmussen 2023: sect. 7). We can now notice, however, that this consideration also applies to Alda’s situation in Option & Brute Luck: the reason why Alda took a gamble in that case must have been that her options were somewhat limited. If she could have acted so as to achieve the best possible outcome of that gamble with certainty, she would have done that. So, a comparative understanding of responsibility for risks incurred seems to be appropriate quite generally. We next need to combine what we learned from Background Risk with the following observation: the choice of what risk attitude in well-being, or vNM utility function, to adopt is itself a risky choice made by the individual. To elaborate, let’s begin by noting that preferences are dispositions to choose. Preferences under risk are therefore dispositions to choose when we don’t know the consequences of our actions. They can thus be understood as complete plans for how to act in any given circumstance. Once I have chosen such a plan and face some given decision problem, all I have to do is implement an algorithm: pick an option that maximizes my vNM utility.26 In making the choice of risk attitude – that is, in ranking all

Since we know about these risks and opportunities when we choose our risk attitude, they are relevantly like the 50% background risk that Alda faces in Background Risk. If she is responsible for her condition then – which she is, if we want to hold her responsible in Option & Brute Luck – so too are those of us who choose to be risk-seeking and end up poorly off “through no fault of their own”. Ultimately, then, my discussion should be interpreted as casting doubt on the usefulness of Dworkin’s (1981) distinction between brute and option luck.27 Take a paradigm case of brute luck: a rock falls from the sky through the roof and hurts a given individual, Frank, while he was resting in his house, leaving him at wL  Δ when he would otherwise have had well-being level wL. Against my proposal of prioritizing Frank’s predicament differently, depending on his risk attitude in wellbeing, one might note: “there is nothing Frank could have done to alter the probability of this happening!” In response, I claim: the normatively significant event is not that a rock hits Frank’s head, but rather that Frank ends up at well-being wL  Δ; and there is something that Frank could have done to alter the probability of the claim that Frank ends up at well-being level wL  Δ. Before the misfortune, we should leave open that Frank’s future might present him with a risky choice involving the possibility of a Δ-loss from wL. If, prior to the rock falling, we assume that Frank is risk-seeking in well-being, that will result in a different (higher) risk of ending up at wL  Δ in the future than if we assume that Frank is risk-averse in well-being. This is my basis for claiming that it is comparatively more urgent to help Frank if he is risk-averse in well-being in this case. In sum, background risks are part of the context within which we make any choice, including our choice of general policy for how risky to be. Recognition of this fact changes our assessment of any misfortune that befalls a given individual in two opposing ways. On the one hand, we will be able to identify some point in time relative to which the claim that “a misfortune of this magnitude eventuates” was a background risk, and also able to identify some choice the individual could have made at that time – including choice of risk attitude in well-being – which would have altered the probability of that risk. On the other hand, the fact that this claim had positive probability to start with is obviously beyond the individual’s control, and this affects the sense in which they can be held responsible for it. option luck distinction attempts to demarcate a clear line between personal responsibility for one’s condition and lack thereof; but there isn’t one. The erosion of this distinction, I suggest, points to a revision to the notion of personal responsibility for one’s condition: it is to be cashed out comparatively, in terms of what degree of priority one is entitled to receive in the given circumstances, relative to other individuals. Thus, Risk-Prioritarian verdicts such as those in Dire and Favourable Circumstances can be supported by considerations of personal responsibility similar to those that motivate the Ex Ante Intuition (II). A Risk-Prioritarian ranking of policies in terms of how good they are socially or morally speaking systematizes such judgements of prioritization based on individual responsibility.

5. Conclusion While weighing people’s well-being by risk attitudes may seem odd at first, I have tried to convey a way of thinking about distributive ethics which makes the proposal quite natural. This approach is impartial in just the right way: enough as to not play favourites, but not so much that it disregards people’s preferences. It can be motivated by interrelated considerations of justifiability to each person and individual responsibility. And it illuminates the philosophical significance of Harsanyi’s social aggregation theorem, while paying heed to the Sen–Weymark critique. I conclude that the Risk-Priority View offers an attractive account for how well-being should be aggregated.

## Abstract

How should we go about collecting evidence when we’re looking to settle some

question? In this thesis, I develop and defend an account of the evaluative and

normative epistemic dimensions intrinsic to the practice of evidence-gathering.

Chapter 1 introduces the topic. Chapter 2 is devoted to laying out the positive

proposal, which makes use of the notions of accuracy and competence to spell

out the conditions under which an act of evidence-gathering is successful,

rational, and skillful. It also shows how the account can be applied to the

simple case of inquiry into polar questions as well as to the more complex

cases of inquiry into wh-questions and subject matters. Chapters 3 and 4

provide arguments for accepting the account. Chapter 3 zooms in on the

central notion of the proposed account, accuracy gain, and argues that such a

notion independently provides the best available measure of information value,

namely the usefulness of a certain piece of information given the aim of settling

a certain question. This is done by showing that accuracy gain fares better than

competing measures from information theory, Bayesian statistics, and decision

theory on a number of fronts. Chapter 4 ﬁrst looks at how the proposed account

fares vis-à-vis three main competing views about the aim of inquiry, arguing

that it emerges as superior in several respects. Then, the Chapter considers

three objections that may be raised against the proposed account, and argues

that these can be met. Chapter 5 concludes by looking at potential avenues for

future research.

## Introduction

This thesis begins with three simple stories:

The Detective. At a summer mansion by the coast, there’s been a

murder. The detective has been called on the phone, and is already

on her way to the crime scene. On the car, she thinks about how

she should proceed. She needs evidence in order to ﬁnd out who

committed the crime. What she is thinking about right now is how

best to collect such evidence. She knows that under interrogation,

sometimes ﬂaws can be found in the professed alibis of guilty indi-

viduals. But for that, one needs to ask the right questions. She also

knows that ﬁnding the murder weapon would be a breakthrough in

the investigation. But for that, one needs to look in the right places.

The Lab. A group of scientists has just received a major grant, which

allows them to pursue their research project. What they now need

to do is gather as much data as possible. The data is collected via

experiments, and the experiments need special equipment. Unfor-

tunately, the grant can only cover the purchase of a limited amount

5


<!-- Page 7 -->


of such equipment. So, they sit down and discuss what experiments

it would be best to pursue.

The Curious Layperson. José just watched a documentary which

sparked in him an interest in the issue of whether human beings

have free will. He decides to read a book to gain more information

on the matter. He knows that this is a controversial topic on which

people have held a variety of views, and that reading diﬀerent books

will plausibly lead him to formulate diﬀerent thoughts on the topic.

After looking at the front cover of a number of books, he is now

thinking carefully about which one to buy.

These three cases share an important feature. The detective, the group of

scientists, and the curious layperson all need to collect evidence so that they

can get closer to, and possibly obtain, the truth about a question that they’re

interested in. They are inquiring into their respective matters, or are about to

engage in such a process of inquiry. Further, they all reasonably ask themselves

how best to pursue their inquiries. They know that their inquiries can go well

or badly, better or worse, depending on what choices they make as to which

sources of evidence to consult: they know that they can make good or bad,

better or worse, choices of evidence-gathering. Cases of this kind will be the

focus of this thesis. To abstract away from the speciﬁcs of the three cases above,

I will be focusing on a rather idealized and simpliﬁed situation, which I call

The Setup. An agent is interested in settling a question, 푄, which I

will call the agent’s research question. The agent can perform one of

a set of mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive acts of evidence-

gathering: acts such that performing them results in the acquisition

of certain pieces of evidence.

6


<!-- Page 8 -->


How should the agent choose? Under what conditions should we say that

the agent chose the right act of evidence-gathering? Under what conditions

should we say that the agent’s inquiry went well? This thesis is concerned with

the evaluative and normative dimensions intrinsic to the practice of evidence-

gathering: with what makes certain inquiries go well and others badly, with

what makes it the case that one ought to perform certain acts of evidence

collection and not others.1 Here’s an initial answer to these questions, given for

the purposes of circumscribing some more the boundaries of the topic of this

thesis: an inquiry going well, and an agent choosing the right act, is to do with

how informative, conclusive, telling, instructive, revealing, illuminating, the

evidence that the agent collects is with respect to the agent’s research question.

This answer is non-committal and incomplete. First, it doesn’t say what it is

for some evidence to be informative, conclusive, telling, etc. Part of the thesis

will be concerned with ﬁlling in these details. Secondly, it doesn’t specify what

the exact relationship is between the evaluative and normative judgements to

be made about a given case and the evidence collected being informative,

conclusive, telling, etc., in that case. Part of the thesis will again be concerned

with ﬁlling in these details.

The evaluative and normative dimensions that I will be interested in are

intrinsic to the practice of evidence-gathering in the sense that they hold inde-

pendently of whatever other evaluative and normative considerations may be

at play in each given case of inquiry. An agent may have, for example, moral or

prudential reasons not to consult a certain source of evidence. In these ways, we

can talk about inquiries going well or badly from a moral or prudential point

While I will end up endorsing a view which links the two very tightly at least with respect to evidence-gathering, it’s important to keep them apart until any substantive points are made.

Let me now zoom out for a moment and consider how the project that I will

pursue in this thesis ﬁts into epistemology as a whole. Any comprehensive

epistemological theory should account for two central aspects of epistemic ac-

tivity. One is belief formation. This aspect has been at the centre-stage of much

of post-Gettier epistemological theorizing. The key questions to ask at this

juncture are: given that a certain agent possesses such-and-such evidence, what

doxastic attitudes should she form? What makes it the case that she should

form precisely those doxastic attitudes in response to that evidence? What

justiﬁes belief? These are among the most fundamental questions in episte-

mology. But an overly narrow focus on them risks suggesting an incomplete

picture of epistemic activity. For it shadows the fact that agents have a degree

of control over what evidence they receive. We get much of our evidence via

perception, simply by navigating our environment and without any conscious

eﬀort directed at collecting it. But sometimes we also decide to look for evidence

bearing on a certain matter, in order to become better informed about it. Nor

is this a feature peculiar to adult human beings: children and non-human an-

imals also actively look for information, such as when a dog uses its olfactory

capacities to individuate the location of a certain object of interest. Following

Jane Friedman, we can call the former kind of evidence acquisition “accidental

learning”, and the latter kind “learning by design”.3 Thus, besides belief for-

mation, epistemic activity involves a second central aspect, evidence collection.

While belief formation concerns doing the best one can given the limited per-

spective on the world that one occupies, evidence collection concerns gaining

a better perspective on the world in the ﬁrst place.

3Friedman (forthcoming b, p. 6). Of course, as Friedman notes, some types of learning may fall in between these two extremes, which are to be seen as generating something like a continuum rather than a strict binary categorization.

My project sits squarely within this second aspect of epistemic activity, evi-

dence collection, or learning by design. There is an important epistemological

issue belonging to this second aspect that I will not be concerned with, how-

ever. This is the issue of whether there are epistemic obligations or duties to

collect evidence in the ﬁrst place. Rather, I look at the question of what choices

an agent should make, and how well an agent’s inquiry goes, granted that our

agent has already decided to collect evidence on the matter. Whether the agent

is under a duty to collect evidence—epistemic or otherwise—is orthogonal to

the issue of whether her inquiry ends up going well, and of whether she makes

the right choices given that inquiry’s aim. I thus remain neutral about the issue

of whether there are any duties to gather evidence, and I do not take my project

to rely on their existence.4

all of them have been defended compellingly by other epistemologists. It will be

within which the positive proposal of Chapters 2, 3, and 4, is to be understood.

your evidence can make a false proposition likely. I will remain non-committal

## Chapter 2

## Evidence-Gathering:

## Accuracy and Competence

In this Chapter, I lay out my account of the evaluative and normative dimensions

intrinsic to the practice of evidence-gathering. I will state the conditions under

which an act of evidence-gathering counts as successful, rational, and skillful,

and will further explore the connections between these three aspects. It takes

little reﬂection to notice that evaluating people’s evidence-gathering choices

is not something conﬁned to the epistemology classroom, but is rather one of

the ways in which we ordinarily hold each other accountable qua intelligent

### 2.1 Initial Remarks

It will be useful to start with some general observations about what kind of

practice evidence-gathering is. First, evidence-gathering is an activity with

an aim, or goal. This plausibly makes evidence-gathering an example of what

Ernest Sosa calls critical domains of value: sets of interrelated entities, activ-

ities, or practices evaluated with respect to a central value, which is valuable

for its own sake relative to that domain.1 Consider as an illustration chess. A

player’s choices can be evaluated vis-à-vis the aim of chess, i.e. checkmating

the opponent. We can say that the player did well or badly, that they should

or shouldn’t have moved a given piece. These evaluative and normative con-

siderations are insulated from moral, prudential or aesthetic evaluations, and

are made possible by the fact that chess is an activity with an aim, or goal.

I will state the aim or goal of evidence-gathering neutrally as improving one’s

epistemic position with respect to one’s question of interest, for example the question

whether 푝. There is a conspicuous literature on what the aim or goal of inquiry

is, which I will turn to consider closely in Chapter 4: knowledge, true belief and

justiﬁed belief are the main contenders.2 In that literature, the aim of inquiry

is often stated in neutral terms as settling a certain question, or as having the

answer to that question, for example the question whether 푝.3 However, this

formulation is too narrow for our purposes. There are cases in which there is

no way for agents to settle whether 푝, but there are ways for them to gain more

information on whether 푝; in such cases, agents may rationally carry out an act

Second, as emerges from this very last point, the aim of evidence-gathering

Third, an act of evidence-gathering is an act in the thick sense of the term,

that it maximises accuracy gain; it is rational to the extent that it maximises

expected accuracy gain; it is skillful to the extent that it manifests the agent’s

evaluative dimensions combine in diﬀerent ways, the best case being one where

the act of evidence-gathering is skillfully successful: it maximises accuracy gain

and expected accuracy gain with respect to the question of interest to the agent

thanks to the agent’s competence at collecting accuracy-maximising evidence.

### 2.4 The Accuracy-Based Virtue-Theoretic Account

We can now state our complete account of the epistemic evaluations surround-

ing the practice evidence-gathering:

The Accuracy-Based Virtue-Theoretic Account.

29

• An act of evidence-gathering is successful to the extent that it maximises

accuracy gain relative to all acts available;

• It is rational to the extent that it maximises expected accuracy gain relative

to all acts available;

• It is skillful to the extent that it manifests the agent’s relevant competence

at gathering accuracy-maximising evidence;

• It is skillfully successful iﬀit maximises accuracy gain and expected ac-

curacy gain thanks to the agent’s competence at gathering accuracy-

maximising evidence.

Two comments about the account are in order. First, while a skillful act

of evidence-gathering may fail to be successful, it plausibly can’t fail to be

rational. In general, how could an agent manifest a competence at choosing the

best option while failing to choose what they themselves should expect to be best

in the given case? More speciﬁcally, at least with competences involving choice,

it is hard to see how scenarios in which what the agent should expect to be best

is in fact best could fail to be in the range relevant for competence-assessment:

the range of counterfactual scenarios that we look at in order to decide whether

the agent’s act is skillful. If the competence is one at choosing the best option,

it will always be relevant to see what happens at worlds in which expectations

match reality. But notice that if the agent chooses irrationally, the disposition

they manifest will lead them astray in such worlds.23 Such a disposition will

therefore not be one to succeed, and won’t qualify as a competence. So there

seem to be quite robust structural reasons for thinking that an irrational act of

evidence-gathering can’t be skillful: even if the irrational act succeeds at the

actual world, the disposition that the act manifests will lead the agent to fail in

## Interlude

Chapter 2 presented the accuracy-based virtue-theoretic account. The purpose of

this brief interlude is to make the reader aware that the arguments of the next

two Chapters will focus on defending primarily the accuracy-based component

of the account. This is the component that stands most in need of support,

and it is also the more distinctively epistemological one. That an evaluative

dimension of competence is called for besides those of success and rationality

emerges quite clearly from the examples of §2.3. What still needs defence is

the claim that accuracy gain, as opposed to some other putative epistemic value,

is required to account for the dimensions of success and rationality in the ﬁrst

place.

This is not to say that my virtue-theoretic interpretation of the examples of

§2.3 cannot be questioned. For example, a more expansive theory of rationality

in terms of reasons-responsiveness arguably accommodates much of the same

data captured by virtue theory.31 Consider again the case in which an agent

chooses the rational option but only as a result of a coin toss. Such a reasons-

My arguments so far have proven particularly damaging for information gain

and probability gain, but KL distance and impact come out as relatively un-

### 3.5 The Argument from Simplicity

The arguments of §3.3 and §3.4 lend support to the accuracy gain model on the

grounds that it is consistent with more intuitions than its rivals and possesses

greater explanatory power. In this section, I want to show that accuracy gain is

also the simplest theory of information value available.

To see this, notice ﬁrst that none of probability gain, information gain,

KL distance, and impact provide an account of objective information value,

alongside what we called expected information value. This is no ﬂaw in its own

right, especially once one bears in mind that these measures have largely been

devised to learn facts about people’s rationality, and what is rational for an agent

to do is standardly assumed to depend entirely on the agent’s own perspective.

Yet as we examine each of these models from a purely theoretical point of view,

asking which of them best accounts for the notion of information value, it makes

sense to ask whether we shouldn’t want them to have something to say about

the objective perspective, too. We can ask: how useful should an agent 푆with

research question 푄and probabilities 푃(·) judge that piece of information 푟is

### 3.7 Conclusion

What is the correct measure of the usefulness of acquiring certain information,

or of asking certain questions in order to acquire certain information, relative to

the aim of settling a given research question? The accuracy gain model stands

out as the best candidate theory of information value: it is simpler, it ﬁts more

intuitions, and it has greater explanatory power than any of the other available

theories. Information value is to be accounted for in terms of accuracy gain.

This provides a strong case for the accuracy-based component of the account

of Chapter 2. It’s clear that agents are successful to the extent that their evidence-

gathering maximises information value, relative to their research question. And

it’s clear that they are rational to the extent that their evidence-gathering max-

imises expected information value, again relative to their research question.

What wasn’t so clear, and stood in need of argument, was the claim that ac-

curacy gain, as opposed to some other putative epistemic value, is required to

account for the dimensions of success and rationality in the correct epistemic

axiology and normativity of evidence-gathering. But we just saw that informa-

tion value is to be accounted for in terms of accuracy gain: the principles of

Generalized Success and Generalized Rationality put forward in §2.6 then

follow, and the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry is vindicated.

## Chapter 4

## A Comprehensive Theory of

## Inquiry

In this Chapter, I compare the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry developed

so far with three main contenders: (i) zetetic veritism, according to which true

belief is the aim of inquiry, (ii) the credal accuracy theory, according to which

improving the accuracy of one’s actual credences is the aim of inquiry, and (iii)

zetetic gnosticism, according to which knowledge is the aim of inquiry. Such a

comparison will bring out the distinctiveness of the account here defended, and

it will also illustrate how the proposed account fares better than the three extant

views in a number of respects. Towards the end of the chapter, I deal with three

objections that may be levelled against my evidential accuracy account.

### 4.1 Two Desiderata

The evidential accuracy account satisﬁes two central desiderata for a satisfatory

theory of inquiry. The ﬁrst one is that it accommodate the fact that evaluative

72


<!-- Page 74 -->


judgements about how well inquiries go are gradable rather than binary. An

inquiry can not only achieve or fail to achieve its aim. Crucially, it can achieve

or fail to achieve its aim to various degrees. We can say that this inquiry went

better than that one, but worse than yet another one. Call this the gradability

desideratum. The second desideratum for a satisfactory theory of inquiry is that

it accommodate the connection between the aim of inquiry and the value of

information. In particular, such a theory should provide a plausible account

of the value of information, which is derived from the theory’s posited aim

of inquiry as follows: information should count as valuable to the extent that

acquiring it helps the agent achieve her inquiry’s aim, as posited by the theory.

Then, this account of information value is to prove competitive when com-

pared to those oﬀered by cognitive psychologists and statisticians. Call this the

information value desideratum.

It is easy to see that the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry meets both

desiderata. We just saw in Chapter 3 how the evidential accuracy theory

provides an account of information value which is not only plausible, but

actually better than the extant accounts. And it is clear that the evidential

accuracy theory delivers evaluative judgements about how well inquiries go

of a suﬃcient ﬁneness of grain. Inquiry goes well (badly), according to the

account, to the extent that the accuracy of the agent’s evidential probability in

the true answer to the given research question increases (decreases), after the

agent acquires some evidence. Since there will be very many such extents, there

will be very many degrees to which an inquiry can go well (badly). I now turn

to look at how alternative proposals about the aim of inquiry fare with respect

to these two desiderata.

### 4.2 Zetetic Veritism

According to what we can call zetetic veritism, outright true belief is the aim

of inquiry.1 As it stands, this view fares especially poorly in relation to our

two desiderata. If the agent acquires the relevant true belief while inquiring,

her inquiry goes well. If the agent doesn’t acquire the relevant true belief,

her inquiry goes badly. We are oﬀered no tools for measuring degrees to

which inquiries can go well or badly, for forming a true belief is an all-or-

nothing matter. Thus zetetic veritism seems unable to meet the gradability

desideratum. If this ﬁrst desideratum isn’t met, there is little hope for the

second desideratum to be satisﬁed either, for the theory will lack the resources

to account for diﬀerent degrees to which information can be valuable, and so

its measure of information value will be a non-starter when compared to the

existing measures.

However, perhaps the zetetic veritist can couple the claim that true belief

is the aim of inquiry with a claim about how to measure closeness to the aim

of inquiry, namely closeness to true belief. If so, the veritist could say that an

agent’s inquiry goes well to the extent that the doxastic attitude that the agent

holds with respect to the true answer to her research question at the end of

her inquiry is close to true belief. The natural proposal is that closeness to true

belief is to be measured by means of accuracy scoring rules. False belief and true

belief would constitute the diametrically opposed endpoints of the “closeness

to true belief” continuum, and in between one would have credences to be

ranked according to their accuracy: the more accurate a given credence is, the

closer to true belief it counts. This reﬁned version of zetetic veritism shares

much with the next proposal about the aim of inquiry that I will consider, the

### 4.3 The Credal Accuracy Theory

According to the credal accuracy theory, the aim of inquiry is to increase the ac-

curacy of one’s credence in the true answer to one’s research question.2 Inquiry

goes well to the extent that the agent’s posterior credence in the true answer

to the research question is accurate. This theory clearly meets the gradabil-

ity desideratum, for there are very many extents to which the agent’s relevant

posterior credence can be accurate.

However, it’s not clear that any interesting notion of information value can

be derived from such a theory. For notice that on this view, any piece of evidence

can be anything from extremely useful to extremely harmful depending on what

the agent makes of it—irrespectively of the agent’s prior credence distribution.

If the agent acquires a piece of misleading evidence and updates on it rationally,

such a piece of evidence will count as of negative value according to the credal

accuracy theory. But the credal accuracy theory will also judge the very same

piece of evidence as of positive value if the very same agent with the very same

prior credences irrationally misinterprets the evidential support relation and

goes on to form a very accurate credence in the true answer to the research

question as a result of acquiring that evidence. One can of course make the

value of information so dependent on facts about the agent’s belief formation,

but this deprives such a notion of much epistemological interest.

of information, relative to a given research question. But we can’t get that

with zetetic gnosticism, for the lack of a shared and clear notion of closeness

to knowledge makes it impossible to devise such a precise value function for

the value of information. By contrast, the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry

oﬀers precisely such a value function, and as we’ve seen in Chapter 3, promises

to ﬁt in with, and provide a plausible interpretation of, cognitive psychologists’

### 4.5 Objections

The evidential accuracy theory of inquiry thus compares favourably in relation

to the three contenders that I have looked at: zetetic veritism, the credal accu-

racy theory, and zetetic gnosticism. To complete my defence of the evidential

accuracy theory, I now turn to consider three objections that might be levelled

against it.

### 4.5.1 Gettier Cases

Consider again Gettier cases. These have been mentioned above to pose prob-

lems for the accuracy of evidence account of closeness to knowledge. The

thought was that agents in Gettier cases have high accurate evidential probabil-

ity and high accurate justiﬁed credence in the true answer, but intuitively count

as being distant from knowing. The gnostic may now accept this point, and

reject the accuracy of evidence account of closeness to knowledge, but raise the

following worry against the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry:

Not only do Gettierized agents count as distant from knowing, they

also intuitively count as distant from the aim of inquiry—whatever

that happens to be. In other words, their inquiry does not intuitively

count as going well. Yet such agents end up with high accurate ev-

idential probabilities and high accurate justiﬁed credences. Hence,

the evidential accuracy theory will classify their inquiries as going

reasonably well.

Here is my response: I agree that something sub-optimal is going on in Gettier

cases, but I question that this shows that the agents’ inquiries in such cases go

any worse than as predicted by the evidential accuracy account.

In particular, it is crucial to notice that Gettier cases are instances of negative

86


<!-- Page 88 -->


introspection (or negative access) failures. According to the principle of negative

introspection, if 푝is not part of one’s evidence, one has conclusive evidence

that 푝is not part of one’s evidence.11 We can see how this principle fails in

Gettier cases: in our example above, the agent’s evidence does not include that

it’s 3 pm, but the agent lacks conclusive evidence that her evidence does not

include that it’s 3 pm. Indeed, her evidence supports that her evidence includes

that it’s 3 pm. Thus, the agent’s evidential probability as to what the time is

will be quite accurate, but her evidential probability as to what’s part of her

evidence will be misleading, i.e. her evidential probability will support the

false proposition that her evidence includes that it’s 3 pm. This rightly makes

for a negative epistemic evaluation of the case: the agent doesn’t fare very well

overall, epistemically speaking. Moreover, as I’ve described the case so far, I’ve

assumed that the agent conforms her credences to her evidential probabilities.

But it’s important to note that negative introspection failures typically result in

failures to be rational: agents in Gettier cases will most likely outright believe that

it’s 3 pm, thus lending more conﬁdence to its being 3 pm than their evidence

warrants. If we’re imagining the case this way, unwarranted outright belief

rightly makes for an additional negative epistemic evaluation of the case: the

agent doesn’t fare very well overall, epistemically speaking. Further, agents

in Gettier cases will also typically hold a number of false beliefs about their

environment: in our case, the agent will presumably falsely believe that the

clock is working. If we’re imagining the case this way, false belief about one’s

surroundings rightly makes for an additional negative epistemic evaluation of

the case: the agent doesn’t fare very well overall, epistemically speaking.

By pointing to these various epistemic dimensions relative to which Get-

tierized agents fare poorly, I submit, we can explain away the judgement that

their inquiries go worse than as predicted by the evidential accuracy account.

### 4.5.2 Merely Statistical Evidence

A similar worry might arise with respect to merely statistical evidence. Lottery

a loser), but intuitively count as being distant from knowing, at least by the

gnostic’s own lights. The gnostic may now accept this point, and reject the

accuracy of evidence account of closeness to knowledge, but raise the following

worry against the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry:

Not only do agents in lottery cases count as distant from knowing,

they also intuitively count as distant from the aim of inquiry—

whatever that happens to be. In other words, their inquiry does

not intuitively count as going well. Yet such agents end up with

high accurate evidential probabilities and high accurate justiﬁed

credences. Hence, the evidential accuracy theory will classify their

### 4.5.3 Inﬁnitary Cases

A ﬁnal objection to the evidential accuracy theory appeals to inﬁnitary cases.

Suppose that some coins have been tossed. Your research question is whether

they all landed heads. You ﬁnd out that the sequence of coin tosses was inﬁnite.

Your evidential probability that they didn’t all land heads increases to 1, once

you update on the information that the sequence was inﬁnite.13 Assume further

that they didn’t in fact all land heads. According to the evidential accuracy

account, you have reached the best possible epistemic position you can occupy

with respect to your inquiry into whether all coins in the sequence landed

heads. However, the objection goes:

You don’t know that they didn’t all land heads; you cannot rule out

that they didn’t; for all you know, they did. There’s more evidence

you can collect which would improve your epistemic position with

respect to your research question. For example, if you found out

that some coins landed tails, that would count as an improvement

in your epistemic position, for you would then know the answer to

your research question.14

I have two main lines of reply to this objection. The ﬁrst one is to note that

it’s debatable whether or not you don’t know that not all coins landed heads,

upon ﬁnding out that the sequence was inﬁnite. Above, I granted the point that

you don’t know of any ﬁnite lottery that your ticket is a loser (before the results

### 4.6 Conclusion

This concludes my defence of the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry. The

theory fares better than its three main contenders with respect to the gradability

and information value desiderata. Moreover, it has the resources to meet some

of the most salient objections. No doubt more could be said on both fronts,

either to defend or attack the evidential accuracy theory. At least for now,

however, the theory emerges as the best one on oﬀer. In the next concluding

Chapter, I will look at potential applications and extensions of the theory after

brieﬂy summarizing what has been accomplished so far.

## Chapter 5

## Conclusions

In this thesis, I have proposed and defended an account of the epistemic ax-

iology and normativity surrounding the practice of evidence-gathering. Let

me brieﬂy summarise each of the account’s building blocks. In the Introduc-

tion, I outlined The Setup, intended to delineate our object of epistemological

study: an agent is interested in settling a question, 푄, and can perform one of

a set of mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive acts of evidence-gathering. I

next presented, in Chapter 2, the accuracy-based virtue-theoretic account, which

speciﬁed the conditions under which such an act of evidence-gathering counts

as successful, rational, and skillful. At the core of the account is the notion

of accuracy gain, which corresponds to the change (positive, negative, or null)

in the accuracy of the agent’s evidential probability in 푄’s true answer that

updating on the evidence collected by performing the chosen act brings about.

The greater the accuracy gain, the more successful the act will be. The greater

the expected accuracy gain, the more rational the act will be. To the extent

that the agent’s act manifests a competence at collecting accuracy-maximising

evidence, it will additionally count as skillful. Finally, if success and rationality

99


<!-- Page 101 -->


are achieved thanks to the agent’s competence, the act will count as skillfully

successful. Chapters 3 and 4 focused on defending the epistemological core

of the accuracy-based virtue-theoretic account, which I called the evidential ac-

curacy theory of inquiry. Chapter 3 argued that accuracy gain independently

provides the best available account of information value. This result provides

strong support in favour of the evidential accuracy theory, for it connects the

success and rationality of an act of evidence-gathering with the usefulness of

the information that the agent obtains by performing it. Chapter 4 looked at

how the evidential accuracy theory fares vis-à-vis three main contenders, argu-

ing that it better ﬁts in with the two desiderata of gradability and information

value and that it can meet three core objections. This concluded my defence of

the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry.

However, it should be clear that my defence of such a theory is only to be

seen as the starting point for epistemological work on the topic of evidence-

gathering. For far from putting to rest philosophical questions about the nature

of inquiry and evidence collection, the account here defended generates yet

more avenues for thought, both by identifying additional problems in the epis-

temology of inquiry itself, and also by connecting the epistemology of inquiry

to other philosophical areas. I now wish to conclude by looking at some of the

avenues for future research suggested by the present account.

that attempting to maximise accuracy gain at each stage in the inquiry is not the

best strategy for the agent to adopt in order to maximise accuracy gain overall.

In general, the best strategy may be one that does not bear its fruits until much

later in the process, but that once it does it delivers beneﬁts so great as to make

up for a middling start. Thus, in cases where the agent faces sequences of

choices, she should take a big-picture view and choose the sequence of acts

recommended by the best strategy, rather than assess each individual choice in

isolation.1 In the case of evidence-gathering, this will mean that our agent will

act rationally to the extent that she chooses those strategies that are expected to

maximise accuracy gain overall. These brief remarks should make it clear that

the evidential accuracy account is capable of being extended from the single

choice case to the much more complex case of sequences of choices. But much

work remains to be done in formally spelling out the details of this extended

approach.

Another limitation of the account as currently developed concerns the em-

pirical question of whether agents choose information in accordance with the

injunction to maximise expected accuracy gain. The ﬁnal section of Chapter 3

tentatively suggested a positive answer, but more research needs to be carried

out for the result to be made robust. Relatedly, if it turned out that agents

choose sources of evidence in an attempt to maximise expected accuracy gain,

how would this conclusion bear on the traditional view in psychology that

people’s thinking is riddled with irrationality?2 Such an “irrationalist” inter-

pretation is now widely thought to rely on obsolete and simplistic models of

how rational agents think or act.3 A very recent research project in episte-

mology attempts to use philosophically sophisticated models of rationality to

vindicate people’s judgements and behaviour against the irrationalist interpre-

tation.4 The ﬁnal section of Chapter 3 again suggests that the present work

ﬁts in nicely with the aims and scope of this research project, but interesting

work remains to be done to see just how much of people’s information-gathering

choices can be vindicated on the assumption that they act in order to maximise

expected accuracy gain. For instance, what is the relation between conﬁrmation

bias and expected accuracy gain maximisation? Questions like this will have to

be addressed in future work.

Other avenues for future research arise not so much from limitations of the

current account, but rather from the connections between the epistemology

of evidence-gathering and other philosophical areas that the account helps to

shed light upon. One such connection is with the philosophy of language.

According to the current account, asking a question can be viewed as an act

of evidence-gathering whose possible outcomes correspond to the question’s

possible answers. Suppose that a group of agents is interested in settling a

certain question, or a set of questions. The current account suggests that given

the purposes of their investigation, there will be pressure on these agents to

praise the posing of questions with high expected accuracy gain, and blame

the posing of questions with low or null expected accuracy gain. By the same

token, the account suggests that there will be incentives for these agents to

praise assertions with useful informational content, and blame assertions with

useless informational content. Thus, it seems that group inquiries can trigger

the activation of norms on posing questions, and of norms on assertion stronger

than the norms on assertion that are ordinarily thought to be in place (e.g. assert

푝only if you know it).5 Interesting future research could result by looking at how

much work these hypothesised norms can do in explaining what questions and

102


<!-- Page 104 -->


assertions count as relevant in a given conversational context.6

A second connection to be explored in future work concerns the conﬁrma-

tion measures proposed in the philosophy of science literature. The current

account has already established a surprising and welcome connection between

accuracy measures and measures of information value. Various measures have

additionally been proposed to account for the amount of support that a given

piece of evidence provides for a given hypothesis; these get called conﬁrmation

measures.7 Some have already established connections between conﬁrmation

measures and accuracy measures on the one hand, and conﬁrmation measures

and information value measures on the other.8 It is thus tempting to put all

these pieces together and explore the prospects for the current account to be

able to provide a unifying treatment of accuracy measures, information value

measures, and conﬁrmation measures.

These are only some of the philosophical uses to which the proposed ac-

count, or some modiﬁed, extended version thereof, can be put. That the account

uncovers so many new areas ripe for philosophical inquiry is itself an additional

argument in its favour, at least according to the abductive methodology that I’ve

assumed throughout this work. The ﬁeld of epistemology has seen, in recent

decades, a desirable expansion from its initial focus on individual belief forma-

tion that characterised so much of the post-Gettier literature to other topics just

as worthy of attention. Central to this expansion are social epistemology, the

theory of rational action, and the topic of epistemic norms. Inquiry has also

been recently re-discovered as an object of proper epistemological theorizing,

which has extended epistemology’s reach once again. With this thesis, I hope

to have contributed somewhat to the study of inquiry, and more generally, to
